## C. C. EDGAR · ZENON PAPYRI III

<note>C.C. Edgar (1870–1938) was a renowned British papyrologist who served as the Secretary-General of the Antiquities Department in Egypt. This volume is part of the monumental "Catalogue Général des Antiquités Égyptiennes du Musée du Caire."</note>

<term>Zenon Papyri: A massive archive of over 2,000 Greek documents from the 3rd century BCE, discovered in the Faiyum region of Egypt. They belonged to Zenon, the business manager for Apollonios, the finance minister of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</term>

# PREFACE.

---

The present volume contains the remainder of the dated papyri (nos. 59298-59374) and a series of undated letters and other documents arranged in alphabetical order according to the names of the correspondents (nos. 59375-59531). In dealing with the former class I have followed the same system of dating as in the two previous volumes. But it is necessary to repeat that when we reach the reign of Ptolemy III <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes, reigned 246–222 BCE.</note>, as the difference between the regnal and the financial year becomes greater, so does the possibility of error. One fact, which has not yet been properly appreciated, shows what a hold the latter system had on the inhabitants of the <term>countryside</term> <note>original: "χώρα" (chora); used here to refer to the Egyptian interior outside of Alexandria.</note>. When demotic <note>A cursive Egyptian script used for legal and administrative documents.</note> documents are dated by two years, e. g. '33, which is also 34', while the first is of course the old Egyptian year, the second is not, as has been assumed, the regnal, but the financial year. Though this to my mind was already evident, a lately published text, *P. S. I.* 1010, D <note>Referring to the "Pubblicazioni della Società Italiana," a major series of papyrological editions.</note>, has placed it beyond doubt.

We have now published the greater and more important part of the Cairo collection. There still remain: 1° several groups of papyri acquired since we began to print the catalogue, one of them not yet thoroughly examined; 2° a long series of accounts, containing much that is interesting; 3° a certain number of letters of which the authors' names are lost, but which are nevertheless fairly intelligible; 4° a mass of smaller fragments. The number of texts either wholly or partly recovered by the piecing together of such fragments is already very large, more so than the reader would suspect from the look of the printed pages; and of the several hundred fragments that are still left one may confidently expect that many will prove to belong to incomplete documents in this and other collections.

The method of publication is described in the introduction to volume I. The plates are again reproduced from the photographs of Mr. F. Oropesa.

<summary>The editor introduces the third volume of the Cairo Zenon Papyri, explaining the transition to undated correspondence and clarifying the complex dating systems used in Ptolemaic Egypt. He notes that while the bulk of the collection is now published, many fragments and accounts remain for future study.</summary>
<keywords>papyrology, Ptolemy III, dating systems, regnal year, financial year, chora, demotic script, Cairo Museum collection, Zenon Archive</keywords>

## ZENON PAPYRI.

**59298. Letter from Rhôdon to Paramonos.** — 0 m. 105 x 0 m. 345. — Date: 12^th^ June, 250 B.C.

Rhodon writes about various purchases which Paramonos had commissioned him to make, three <term>choes</term><note>A chous was a liquid measure approximately equal to 3.2 liters.</note> of honey, a mattress for which he had given earnest-money <note>A down payment or deposit to secure a contract.</note> without as yet obtaining the article, and a pig for the festival of Arsinoe. The date of the letter is established by no. 59305, which deals with the same subject. Paramonos is styled <term>hoplomachos</term><note>original: "ὁπλόμαχος"; a military instructor or one who fights with heavy armor.</note> on the back (cf. no. 59488), and it is noticeable that he dates his own letter by the Macedonian calendar. It is not certain whether he is the same Paramonos who appears sometimes as a colleague of Thrason (nos. 59130, 59449) and to whom Apollonios in no. 59179 sends an order concerning a trespass made by the <term>cleruchs</term><note>Soldier-settlers who were granted plots of land by the state.</note> on his <term>dorea</term><note>original: "δωρεά"; a large estate granted as a gift by the king to a high official.</note> in the Memphite <term>nome</term><note>An administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note>.

Rhodon to Paramonos, greetings, and to the young servants. Three <term>choes</term> of honey have been bought for you.
<margin>Write then</margin>
to me to whom I should deliver it. And concerning the mattress, having given a deposit, we nearly
<margin>lost it.</margin>
For although Zenon wrote to Jason to give a mattress or 30 <term>drachmae</term><note>The symbol ⊢ represents the drachma, the standard silver coin.</note>, he did not give it.
<margin>Let him write</margin>
therefore to Apollodoros, the one in charge of the sheep, to give 30 <term>drachmae</term> worth of wool, and I
<margin>have decided</margin>
5 here, so that a mattress may be made for you; and I will provide the expenditure. There has also been bought for you
<margin>also</margin>
the sacrificial animal for the festival of Arsinoe for 12 <term>drachmae</term>. You, therefore, petition Zenon so that, as his own...

*Line 1. young servants*<note>original: "παιδαρίοις"</note>: perhaps boys who were being trained by Paramonos; cf. no. 59488, 2.
*Line 4. I have decided*<note>original: "ἀπέγνωσα"</note>: so in the original. *so that [it] may be made* depends on *to give wool*, the intervening clause, *and I have decided here*, being parenthetical.

# 59299. Letter from Euempolos to Zenon. — 0 m. 11 X 0 m. 255. — Date: 23rd June, 250 B.C.

Euempolos writes about sending Zenon supplies of garlic and about the cultivation of garlic in the neighbourhood of Philadelphia <note>A village in the Fayoum founded by Ptolemy II</note>. Two kinds in particular are mentioned, *the Tloic* <note>original: τὰ Τλωικά</note>, the sort grown at Tlos in Asia Minor, and *the Oasitic* <note>original: τὰ Ὀασιτικά</note>, the sort grown in one or other of the western oases, not the Fayoum. The letter, like the following one, though received on the 6th of Pachons, year 36, is dated Pachons 2, year 25, a date which it seems impossible to explain except as an error on the part of Euempolos. It seems probable from the phraseology that Zenon was away from Philadelphia when the letters were written, though within four day's journey; he may perhaps have been staying at Memphis.

Euempolos to Zenon, greetings. You wrote to me that the garlic at "The Rock" <note>original: τῆς πέτρας</note>
is pleasing to you,
and if the garlic with me is of the same kind, that it should be available for the shipments. Now, the garlic with me,
being late-ripening, will be available for planting. For when you ordered at that time that Herakleides should give me the land,
he gave the order to Harmodios, and he himself sailed down with you, and Harmodios sailed with Chairigenes. By dragging his feet <note>original: παρέλκων</note>
<margin>5</margin> and not handing over the land at the proper time, he caused the planting to be late. And you wrote
to Theopompos to send you half Tloic and half Oasitic. Therefore, none was planted

*Line 1. The Rock* <note>original: τῆς πέτρας</note>: a locality at the edge of the desert near Philadelphia (cf. no. 59172, 17).
*Line 2. that it should be available* <note>original: ἵνα ὑπάρχηι</note>: indirect imperative, depending on *you wrote*.
*Line 3. Herakleides*: the farmer of the 10,000 arourai <note>An aroura is a unit of land area, roughly 0.6 acres</note> (see no. 59292, 420).
*Line 4.* I do not know whether this excursion was a result of the invitation of no. 59282 to the feast in honour of the king. For Harmodios and Chairigenes see vol. II, index V.

# 59300. Letter from Euempolos to Zenon. — 0 m. 175 X 0 m. 255. — Date: 23rd June, 250 B.C.

Euempolos reports that with Herakleides’ approval he had been inspecting the vineyards and making a census of the persons who had planted vegetables in them, in order that they should pay the *half-share tax* <note>term: hemiseuma (ἡμίσευμα) — a tax or rent consisting of half the produce</note>, as usual, on a joint valuation of the crops. The only man who objected was Apollonides, who declared that he would not allow him to enter his vineyard. But Apollonides would not be talking in this foolish way if he had been made to pay the proper amount for the sub-letting of the hundred-aroura vineyard. For whereas Euempolos had obtained 20 and 41 drachmæ for quite small areas, putting them up to auction in the regular way, Apollonides had made a private arrangement with certain persons and then announced that he had let the whole for 50 drachmæ; and he even made them a present of the grapes that were left. Euempolos proceeds to say that nobody is putting the old wine-vats in order or building new ones, although the vintage is drawing near, nor are they making ready to catch the mice. So unless Zenon comes at once and gives his orders, he will find himself much behindhand. Several points in this text are difficult to understand and I doubt if Rostovtzeff’s explanation is correct (*Large Estate*, p. 98). He supposes lines 8–14 to refer to the farming of the produce of the vineyards and says that Apollonides received much more money from the operation than Euempolos. But the point of the story is that he received much *less* in proportion to the size of the vineyard and that he ought by rights to have been forced to pay the difference between what he obtained and what he ought to have been obtained. Again, the sums mentioned are far too small

to represent the value of the produce. It seems to me therefore more probable that the passage refers to the sub-letting of those portions of the vineyards in which vegetables could be grown. The vineyards, whether they belonged to cleruchs <note>Soldiers granted land by the state</note> or to the estate, were being exploited by Zenon, who leased them to vine-dressers such as the Herakleides of no. 59269; and the complaint against Apollonides is that he did not obtain proper value for the ground which was sub-leased to the vegetable-growers.

Euempolos to Zenon, greetings. Regarding those who planted the vineyards on a share-basis for
the <term>25th year</term> <note>original: "κε L". L is a symbol for "year".</note>
I requested, having taken an assistant from Herakleides, to make an inspection, so that those who had planted

or gourds or onions or anything else I might register, so that by valuation,

rounds and to prevent me. Rightly then does it occur to Apollonides to talk nonsense; for if the
deficits <note>original: "διάφορα". Referring to the financial shortfall.</note>, just as you said then, from the sale of the hundred-aroura <note>An aroura is about 2/3 of an acre.</note>
vineyard
had been collected, he would not now be talking nonsense in vain. For when I sold, in the plots of
Python,
<margin>10</margin> not even 5 (arouras) for <term>20 drachmae</term> <note>original: "ͱ κ"</note>, and in those of Neoptolemos, if very many,
7 (arouras) for <term>41 drachmae</term> <note>original: "ͱ μα"</note>,

Line 1. <term>25th year</term> : see no. 59299, introduction.
Line 2. Herakleides : probably the overseer of the estate (no. 59292, 420).
Line 4. the half-share : probably the Government tax, collected by Zenon's agents. In a letter published by Collart and Jouguet in the *Raccolta Lumbroso*, p. 123, the same word is used of a tax on the vines themselves.
Lines 4-5. approved of my doing so : 'approving my action'.
Line 8. deficits : translated as 'the amount of the sale' in *P.S.I.*, 434. I take it rather to mean the difference or deficit. Cf. *P. Teb.*, I, p. 63, note 1.
Lines 9-10. Python and Neoptolemos were probably the owners of the vineyards, though these were being exploited by Zenon.
Line 10. <term>20 drachmae</term> : not to be understood as 20 drachmae per unit. Twenty drachmæ was the total sum obtained.

From Euempolos regarding the

Line 11. Anosis : the <term>village scribe</term> <note>original: "κωμογραμματεύς"</note> of Philadelphia, the official interpreter between Greeks and natives. — that man : read <term>ekeinos</term>.
Lines 13-14. Apollonides seems to have allowed the cultivators to help themselves freely to the grapes, but I do not understand the whole passage. What is the meaning of leaving fresh grapes for the <term>Isieia</term>, which fell in the middle of winter? Or has Euempolos confused the <term>Isieia</term> with the <term>Arsinoeia</term> <note>A festival for Queen Arsinoe.</note>?
Line 17. the mice : for other allusions to the depredations of mice see SCHNEBEL, *Landwirtschaft*, p. 274.
Line 18. give orders : 'come to an agreement'. Vitelli reads "you give orders", which gives equally good sense. — attending to other matters : not 'stimulating the rest of them', as Rostovtzeff translates, but 'through attending to other matters'. Zenon was away from home at this time.

### 59301. Memorandum to Zenon from Kassandros. — 0 m. 15 x 0 m. 325. —
Date : June-July, 250 B. C.

Kassandros reminds Zenon about a certain Egyptian about whom he had already spoken to him in Alexandria. This man was one of the peasants from Psychis in

the Memphite nome <note>A 'nome' was an administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note> who had been taken to Philadelphia to work at the harvest, and Zenon had promised to let him go.
The phrase *and in the city* <note>original: "καὶ ἐμ πόλει"</note> implies that the request was written in the country after Kassandros had returned from town. He calls himself ‘one of the soldiers of Apollonios’, which recalls the phrase *of the soldiers from you* <note>original: "τῶν παρὰ σοῦ στρατιωτῶν"</note> of no. 59140. Perhaps Apollonios in virtue of his office maintained a certain number of soldiers, as some minor officials in later times appear with a guard of *fighters* <note>original: "μάχιμοι"; see P. Teb., 112, 81, note</note>; or he may, like Chrysermos of no. 59355 and *P. S. I.*, 513, have been one of the so-called eponymous commanders, whose status has not yet been satisfactorily explained.

Memorandum to Zenon from Kas<gloss>san</gloss>dros, of the soldiers of Apollonios;
concerning [ . . . ]eutos, whom I also mentioned to you in the city, saying that he had been
taken to Philadelphia among the harvesters from the Memphite
village of Psychis. You would do well then to release him, just as
5 you promised me in the city. For the man is useful to us.
->Farewell. Year 36, Pachons.<- <note>Pachons was a month in the Egyptian calendar; Year 36 refers to the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</note>

VERSO :

->Kassandros. To Zenon.<-

*Lines 2-4. concerning . . . Psychis :* these words seem to depend on *memorandum*, but it is sometimes difficult to decide where the title ends and the memorandum itself begins. I follow the usual punctuation.
*Line 3. Cf. P. Hib., 44 and P. S. I., 440, 6, Leontiskos therefore, having forced us, sent us to the harvest.* <note>original: "Λεοντίσκος οὖν ἡμᾶς βιασάμενος ἀπέστειλεν ἐπὶ τὸν θερισμόν."</note> Apparently peasants could be impressed for work on Apollonios’ estates as well as on Crown land. It is possible, however, that Psychis lay in his Memphite property.

### 59302. Fragment of a contract(?). — 0 m. 10 x 0 m. 095. — Date : 19th July, 250 B. C.

Written along the fibres. The text, of which we have only a fragment, may have been a contract about some work at Philadelphia. On the verso is a list of wine-jars with their prices. It appears from this that the <term>hemikadion</term> <note>A liquid measure, literally a 'half-jar'.</note> contained as a rule about three <term>choes</term> <note>A 'chous' was a liquid measure roughly equal to 3 liters.</note> and that the wine, probably in this case local wine, cost about a <term>drachma</term> <note>A standard silver coin.</note> the chous; but there is considerable variation both in the capacity of the jars and in the price of the wine. A. Segré, in discussing this and similar questions (*Studi ital. di Filologia classica*, V, pp. 93 seqq.), is inclined to forget that pottery—

### 59304. Letter from Protarchos to Zenon. — 0.145 m x 0.29 m. — Date: 31st August, 250 B.C.

Protarchos writes that, as Zenon had promised to send them a quantity of natron <note>a naturally occurring mineral salt used as a cleaning agent</note>, they had ordered none themselves and the supply in the district <note>the 'nome' or administrative province</note> being finished they were obliged to travel about and obtain what they could from other districts. He asks Zenon therefore to send for the natron at once, in order that the linen-cleaners may be able to continue their work.
We hear again of the <term>linen-cleaners</term> <note>original: "λινυφοί"</note> in *P.S.I.*, 349 and 566, where the Aphroditopolite financial officer tries to obtain for them a large quantity of linseed oil. This was probably for mixing with the natron to make a sort of soap. Rostovtzeff's suggestion (*Large Estate*, p. 92) that the <term>linen-cleaners</term> were makers of linseed oil seems less likely. They seem to have been a big corporation working under Government control in connection with the weaving industry. I cannot say who Protarchos was or where he wrote from.

Protarchos to Zenon, greetings. Because you promised to send us
[[. . . . . . . . . .]] the <unclear>6</unclear> <note>Possibly 6 talents of natron.</note> [. . . . . .] . . . [. . .] . . . [. . . . . . . . . . . . . . .] . . . . . . . .
[. .] . <unclear>6</unclear> [. . .].

# 59307. Memorandum to Zenon from Dionysios. — 0.22 m x 0.075 m. — Date: 5th October, 250 B.C.

Dionysios reports that he has gone to Koitai to guarantee payment of fifty <term>drachmae</term> <note>the standard silver coin of the Greek world</note> on behalf of Ptolemaios, Zenon having ordered him to ask for five days in which to pay the money. He requests Zenon to give his brother three mattocks to enable them to water the holding in good time.

Dionysios is probably to be identified with the author of *P. S. I.*, 577, a farmer whom Zenon employed to cultivate the <term>kleroi</term> <note>plots of land allotted to military settlers</note> which he was exploiting. He is mentioned again in *P. S. I.*, 432.

### 59308. Letter from Zenon(?) to Axates. — 0.155 m. x 0.29 m. — Date: September or October, 250 B.C. (plate I).

The letter bears no address on the back and does not seem to have been dispatched.
A number of words, letters and figures are scribbled here and there; for the front see plate I; on the back: *toto-to tislone-dume* <note>These appear to be nonsensical scribbles or practice writing</note>.
The first word looks like "To Zenon" <note>original: "Ζήνωνι"</note> rather than "Zenon" and is in rather smaller characters than the rest of the text; above it is written "To Zenon... greeting" <note>original: "Ζήνωνι χ[[.....]]"</note>; and some letters have apparently been deleted before the name Axates. It is therefore doubtful whether "Zenon," or "To Zenon," belongs to the original text and whether Zenon was actually the author.
The writer reminds his correspondent about the priest of Thoeris <note>The Egyptian goddess Taweret, depicted as a hippopotamus, protector of childbirth</note> in Philadelphia, to whom an allowance of twelve <term>drachmae</term> <note>a unit of silver currency</note> a year was due from the priest of Thoeris in some place not specified. The temple in Philadelphia seems to have been affiliated to a larger temple elsewhere, which provided a small sum for the maintenance of the cult. Philadelphia was full of little temples, partly or wholly founded by Apollonios <note>The finance minister of Egypt and Zenon's employer</note> and dedicated to a motley collection of deities. It is not clear how they were all endowed, but there is evidence that portions of Apollonios’ estates were assigned to certain gods. Of Axates nothing is known, unless he be identical with Axapes mentioned in a Michigan papyrus as the royal scribe <note>original: "βασιλικὸς γραμματεύς" — a high-ranking provincial official</note> of the Oxyrhynchite 

<column-break/>

<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>
<page-num>13</page-num>

district <note>original: "nome"</note>; and as Thoeris was the chief deity of Oxyrhynchos, the identification is certainly tempting.

> Zenon to Axates, greetings. We wrote to you even before
> concerning Kollythos the priest of Thoeris in Philadelphia, that there be paid
> to him the amount due from the priest of Thoeris to the temple in
> Philadelphia, but you wrote back to me that there was due to him for the
> <margin>5</margin> year 12 drachmae. No one, then, is paying anything. You, therefore, give orders for
> all the amounts owed to be paid to him; for from these they perform
> the sacrifices.
> ->Farewell. Year 36,<-
> ->Mesore.<-

*Line 2. that there be paid <note>original: "ἀποδίδοσθαι"</note>:* indirect imperative.
*Line 7. they perform <note>original: "ποιοῦνται"</note>:* i. e., the priest and his acolytes.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Museum Entry Journal, no. 48756; P. Edgar*, 47; *Sammelbuch*, 6753.

### 59309. Letter from Nikandros and Peisikles to Zenon. — 0.15 m. x 0.325 m. — Date: about 17th October, 250 B.C.

Nikandros and Peisikles had already written to Zenon to thank him for having arranged about the money due to them, and they now ask him to collect as much of it as he thinks convenient before Diotimos sails up. They ask him also to dispose of the house and the vineyard as soon as possible, in order that they may suffer no loss from this source either.
This letter is a continuation of *P.S.I.*, 375, in which the two partners give more details about the money. They were evidently land-holders, for Zenon had told them that it was impossible to recover the price of the sesame from the bank, and probably they lived in Alexandria entrusting their local interests to Zenon. It is doubtful, however, whether Peisikles is the treasurer who appears so often in the earlier documents.

> Nikandros and Peisikles to Zenon, greetings. If you are well, it would be good; we
> ourselves are also healthy. We wrote to you previously thanking you
> that you would manage the matter of the copper money owed to us, and now
> you will do well, before Diotimos sails up, to take care that you 
> <margin>5</margin> recover from the copper money owed whatever seems to you to be appropriate.

*Line 4. Diotimos:* the <term>hypodioiketes</term> <note>a deputy finance minister</note>, whose visit was probably connected with the settlement of Government claims.

# 59310. Letter from Artemidoros to Zenon. — 0.12 m. x 0.32 m. — Date: October, 250 B.C.

A badly preserved letter from Artemidoros the physician, probably written in Alexandria. He has heard that Petos the swineherd has run away and that a great many pigs are missing. (The herd seems to have belonged to Artemidoros himself). He therefore asks Zenon to have inquiries made as to where Petos has fled and to see that the securities <note>The "guarantors" or "sureties" who were legally responsible for Petos's conduct.</note> are either jailed or bailed until satisfaction has been obtained. At the end he acknowledges receipt of a pig which Zenon has sent him, perhaps for the Arsinoeia <note>A festival in honor of Queen Arsinoe II.</note>.

Artemidoros to Zenon, greeting. If you are well, it would be good; I too am well.
Klaitorios wrote that Petos <gloss>the</gloss> swineherd has run away, leaving behind 6 sacrificial animals <note>original: "ἱερεῖα" — often refers to pigs specifically raised for religious sacrifice.</note> and [.]
young pigs.
He held for us 400 <note>original: "ῡ"</note> rent-producing sacrificial animals [full-grown, and] he owed [additional] young pigs
toward the rent <note>term: "phorus" — the fixed amount of produce or money paid by a tenant.</note> of the pigs.
You would therefore do well to make haste so that the man may be searched for [to see] where he has
run away,
<margin>5</margin> so that so many sacrificial animals do not fail us; and as for the guarantors who have stood surety for
him,
[take care] so that they may either be arrested and led away or give bail until justice is done to us.
We have also received the sacrificial pig which you sent us.
->Farewell. Year 36, Loios [.] 5.<-

*Line 2. Klaitorios: see a note by Viereck in the Raccolta Lumbroso, p. 258.*
*Line 3. The figure 400 <note>original: "ῡ"</note> is doubtful, but the ending of the word for "pigs" seems to me nearly certain.
Petos had no doubt hired the pigs and paid a yearly rent in kind. "Rent-producing" <note>original: "ἔμφορα"</note> means "paying rent".*
*Line 6. "arrested": the middle of the Greek word has been corrected from a different verb ending.*

# 59311. Letter from Artemidoros to Zenon. — 0.11 m. x 0.32 m. — Date: about 25th October, 250 B.C.

Artemidoros the physician writes from Alexandria about some honey which he had requested Zenon to buy for a friend of his called Apollonios living up the river at Ptolemais <note>Likely Ptolemais Hermiou in Upper Egypt.</note>. The honey was to be handed over to Ptolemaios, an agent of Artemidoros, who was to meet a certain Herakleodoros on his way up the river and deliver it to him. It is evident from the context that the Ptolemais mentioned here was the city in Upper Egypt. The papyrus is in very bad condition.

### 59314. Letter from Aristandros to Zenon. — 0.16 m. x 0.33 m. — Date: 8th November, 250 B.C. (plate II).

Aristandros reproaches Zenon for not having sent Herakleides the <term>sitologos</term> <note>a state official responsible for the collection and storage of grain in public granaries</note> as he had promised and urges him to send him now without delay, as Agenor is making trouble and Aristandros is afraid of being brought to book. He adds a sentence about the sesame accounts, saying he has inserted a note that most of the receipts submitted by Zenon come from people who already owed money for corn. Comparing various other texts in which Aristandros is mentioned, particularly *P. S. I.*, 361, 425, 544 and *P. Lille* I, 49 and 50, I think there is little doubt that he was at this time chief <term>oeconome</term> <note>the chief financial officer of a province or district</note> of the Arsinoite province. Agenor we know to have been the <term>strategos</term> <note>the military governor and highest administrative authority</note> of the nome <note>a district or province in Egypt</note> for many years, and the cause of the present trouble may perhaps have been some dispute between the cleruchs <note>soldier-settlers granted land by the state</note> and the Treasury. That, however, is a mere conjecture. Nor do I understand clearly to what transaction the parenthesis about the sesame refers. It may be that the receipts were for the sesame crop on certain lands under Zenon's control (cf. no. 59223) and that he had not noticed that some of the cultivators already owed money to the Treasury.

Aristandros to Zenon, greetings. You should have, just as you agreed
with us, sent Herakleides the <term>sitologos</term>. Nevertheless, even

*Line 2. Herakleides:* in *P. S. I.*, 588 a certain Herakleides appears in connection with Zenon and Agenor, but there is nothing to show whether he was the same person as is mentioned here.

### 59315. Letter from Pekysis to Zenon. — 0.135 m. x 0.16 m. and 0.135 m. x 0.155 m. — Date: 13th November, 250 B.C.

Pekysis writes that Aristandros has ordered him to collect 1500 drachmae for the <term>phorologos</term> <note>a tax-collector</note>. He had already talked to Zenon about a payment of 120 drachmae 1 obol 1 chalkous <note>small copper coins; there were 8 chalkoi to an obol and 6 obols to a drachma</note> on behalf of the cleruchs whose land was being worked by Onnophris and he now asks him to help to have this sum paid as part of the 1500 drachmae. He goes on to speak of the sesame, saying that Herakleides’ people are unwilling to make the distribution without an order from Herakleides himself. Zenon should therefore tell Herakleides to write to the operators to measure out the sesame according to the apportionment proposed by Onnophris. I take the last sentence to refer to the distribution of sesame seed, but it is not easy to grasp the exact import of these various transactions. *P. S. I.*, 603 is perhaps another letter on the same subject, though the meaning and construction of the first sentence are not quite clear.

Pekysis to Zenon, greetings. Aristandros wrote to us from the city <note>original: "ἐκ πόλεως," likely referring to Krokodilopolis, the capital</note> that I should
collect 1500 for the tax-collector. Know also [that] I spoke with you about the 165... <note>The editor's summary notes 120 drachmae, but the Greek text ρξε̄ indicates 165</note>
on behalf of

*Line 1. From the city:* probably Krokodilopolis, as Aristandros does not seem to have been in Alexandria at this time.
*Lines 2-3. On behalf of the soldiers:* cf. no. 59297, 26.

## 59317. Letter to Zenon from Horos. — 0.175 m x 0.125 m. — Date: November 13, 250 B.C. (plate III).

Horos states that he must measure the works carried out over the last nine months and will need four papyrus rolls—three for the building account and one for the vine-dressers' work. Four months’ pay was due, but having received ten drachmae and owing fifteen elsewhere, he asks Zenon for the remaining fifteen drachmae balance. ## 59318. Letter from Onnophris to Zenon. — 0.26 m x 0.055 m. — Date: 28th November, 250 B.C.

Zenon had asked how much hay they had bought on the land of Andromachos, and Onnophris (see no. 59315, 3) replies that they had grazed and reaped 12 3/8 <term>arourai</term> <note>an aroura was a standard Egyptian measure of land, roughly 0.6 acres</note>. Hay when used for pasture would naturally be sold by the <term>aroura</term>, while dry hay was usually reckoned by the <term>desme</term> <note>a bundle</note> of two <term>minae</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1 kg</note>.

> we grazed

> Farewell.

## 59319. Duplicate account. — 0.075 m x 0.07 m. — Date: about 10th January, 249 B.C. (plate III).

A short account addressed to Pindaros and dated by the Macedonian calendar. It gives a list of various articles belonging to various people, with prices attached. Some of the words are abbreviated and not very easy to read. For want of a better explanation I suggest that the list represents a small consignment of goods sent

<column-break/>

<page-num>23</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

by boat to Alexandria to be delivered to certain people, from whom the skipper or supercargo would receive the price. Compare for instance nos. 59015 and 59148.

> 1 For Apollonios, 220 <term>keramia</term> <note>standard pottery jars</note>; for Charidemos,
> 2 <term>kaunakai</term> <note>thick, shaggy woolen cloaks of Persian style</note>, ... 30 <term>minae</term> [weight?] plus 37 1/2 [drachmae?],
> a woman's tunic, 40 drachmae, 1 pair of socks, 4 drachmae;
> for Konon, a cloak, 25 drachmae.
> 5 **Year** 36, Dios 4.
> For Apollonios, 220 <term>keramia</term>; for Charidemos,
> 2 <term>kaunakai</term>, ... 30 <term>minae</term> [weight?] plus 37 1/2 [drachmae?],
> a woman's tunic, [[40]] drachmae, a pair of socks,
> 1 pair, 4 drachmae; for Konon, a cloak, 25 drachmae.
> 10 **VERSO**: To Pindaros.

<margin>*Line 1. 220 keramia*: this is a possible reading of the duplicate in line 6, but it is difficult to make anything out of the abbreviation in line 1.</margin>

<margin>*Line 2. po( )*: I thought of <term>olyra</term> <note>emmer wheat</note>, but Hunt’s suggestion of <term>porphyroi</term> <note>purple</note> seems preferable based on the handwriting. As the <term>kaunakes</term> was a very heavy garment (Aristophanes, *Wasps*, 1147, "it has easily swallowed a talent of wool"), thirty <term>minae</term> is just conceivable as the weight of two; in that case the 37 1/2 drachmae would be the price. It is harder to believe that the thirty <term>minae</term> can be part of the price; surely that would be excessive. Another possible reading, likewise suggested by Hunt, is 30 <term>minae</term> of lead; this fits less well with the context of clothing, but may be right nevertheless.</margin>

**BIBLIOGRAPHY**: *Museum Entry Journal*, no. 48767.

## 59320. Account of corn freight. — 0.295 m x 0.095 m. — Date: about 28th January, 249 B.C.

A short account dealing with the transport of corn from the Arsinoite <note>modern Fayum</note> district to Alexandria (compare *P. Hibeh*, 110). It was no doubt drawn up in the latter place. Written along the fibers and folded horizontally.

> 1 **Year** 36, Dios 22.
> There was calculated for Inaros, son of Phamunis,
> the freight for the merchant ship *Isis*,
> for the grain brought down...

<margin>*Line 2.* For the <term>cybaea</term> <note>a type of merchant vessel</note> see no. 59002, 3. *Isis* was probably the name of the ship, like that in Lucian, *The Ship*, chapter 5: "the prow having the goddess for whom the ship is named, Isis, on either side." In *P. Lille* I, 22 we find a boat described as a "rowing-vessel of the Queen"; but while the editors take "Queen" to be the name of the boat, Wilcken supposes the queen to have been the owner (*Archive for Papyrus Research*, V, p. 226).</margin>

**59323. Copy of a letter from Lysagoras to Diomedes.** — 0.22 m $\times$ 0.11 m. — 250-249 B.C. (plate IV).

Diomedes had apparently brought an action against Bion for a sum of 468 drachmae. How far the proceedings had already gone is not clear, but in the present letter Lysagoras formally undertakes to produce Bion in Alexandria in the office or court of Apollonios or, if he fails to do so, to pay to Diomedes the said sum in the month of Audnaios, provided that he be not called away on Government business. Compare the contract *P. Hib.*, 92, in which the guarantor undertakes to produce the defendant before the <term>strategos</term> <note>a high military and civil governor</note> by a certain date or, failing that, to pay the sum claimed himself.

-> Copy of the letter <-
-> of Lysagoras. <-

-> Lysagoras to Diomedes <-
-> greetings. I guarantee... <- <note>original: "ἐγδέχ[ο]μαι"</note>

# 59325. Agricultural account. — 0.31 m. X 0.20 m. — Date: 249 B.C.

A list of <term>cleruchs</term> <note>military settlers who received land grants in exchange for service</note> in various places, to whom the rest of the rent for year 36 is due to be paid. No doubt Zenon had leased their holdings and had been cultivating them by means of his own farmers. The rent was paid partly in wheat and partly in barley; but sometimes the landlord preferred to have a portion of it commuted into money at the rate of seven <term>artabae</term> <note>a dry measure of roughly 30-40 liters</note> of wheat to the tetradrachm and about five artabae of barley to the drachma. The text shows what a large share Zenon took in the management of these military land grants.

->Column I.<-

To those whom the remainder
of the rent <term>ekphorion</term> <note>rent paid in kind (produce)</note> for Year 36 must be paid:
To those from Memphis:
To Zoilos: [wheat] 8 1/2 1/3 1/8 [artabae]
5 Barley: 42 artabae
To Hegemon: [wheat] 29 1/8 [artabae]
Barley: 40 1/2 1/3 artabae
To Aineas: [wheat] 30 1/8 [artabae]
Barley: 56 artabae
10 | [Total wheat]: 68 1/4 artabae
Barley: 138 1/2 1/3 artabae
To those near the settlement
of Andromachos

*Line 3. To those from Memphis*: see document no. 59297, line 22, "of the elders from Memphis who have been measured land near Tanis" and *P.S.I.* 627, a list of the elder soldiers from Memphis, in which we find the three men mentioned here.
*Line 4.* The measure employed in these calculations is probably the "receiver's measure" <term>dochikon</term>.

**59326. Account. — 0.21 m X 0.355 m. — Date: probably 249 B.C. (plate V).**

Written both on the front and back in a more or less cursive <note>handwriting where letters are joined</note> hand. It is a long account of money paid out for various purposes to various persons connected with Zenon <note>The manager of the vast estate of Apollonios, the finance minister of Egypt</note>. Many of the names are familiar, besides those to which I have given references in the notes, but it is not yet possible to determine the relations of all these people to Zenon and to each other. Some of them are paid farmers, some <term>cleruchs</term> <note>Soldier-settlers granted land by the king</note>, some slaves and domestic servants; and the entries give a good idea of the varied matters of business with which Zenon's accountants had to deal.

To [Arte]midoros son of Sochares, for <term>croton</term> <note>Castor-oil plants, used for lighting and medicine</note> — 100 drachmae
[and] to Philippos son of Ep.....os, as he
5 [assi]gned — 50 drachmae

Line 1. Arbichis: mentioned again in no. 59355, 79. Probably one of the farmers employed by Zenon. The date may perhaps be restored as year 37; compare line 140.

Line 3. For this person see *P.S.I.*, 555, the right date of which is year 37, not 27.

## 59327. List of silver vases held as security. — 0.325 m x 0.37 m. — Date: 249 B.C. (pl. VI).

The practice of raising a little ready money by pawning silver plate is frequently referred to in the Zenon papyri, but this is the most complete document on the subject. It is a long, confused, and much corrected account of money lent on silver plate and of the interest payable on the loans. The vases were deposited in Philadelphia, Memphis, and Alexandria, and various agents of Zenon or Apollonios are mentioned as taking part in the transactions, especially Theopompos, Krotos (see *P. S. I.*, 608), and Sosos. In column 2 we find Krotos holding the securities, but in column 3 and on the back side the vases are apparently deposited at a bank, which lends the money. It is not clear what Zenon’s connection was with these loans, and indeed there are many obscure points in the account. The interest charged varies from two to four per cent per month. From the second account in column 1 we can infer that a sum of 234 1/2 or 240 drachmae was lent on a vase weighing 262 drachmae; the loan described on the back side seems to have been on a less generous scale, but the figures are not quite certain.

->Column I.<-

List of the drinking cups
deposited as security <note>original: "ἐνέχυρα"; collateral for a loan</note> in Philadelphia

<margin>
Line 2. "Deposited as security": this also appears in the title on the back side.
</margin>

*Lines 100-116.* A continuation of the lower part of column 3.

## 59328. Account of goats. — 0 m. 26 x 0 m. 30. — Date: February-March, 248 B.C.

This is an account drawn up by Hermias, a goatherd who is mentioned in several other texts. He leased a large number of goats from Zenon, paying him a yearly rent of four obols <note>a small silver coin</note> and one kid for each goat. The remaining kids became his own property, which he could dispose of as he pleased, and he sold for his own profit the milk and cheese obtained from the goats and perhaps also the hair, which was used for making a coarse cloth (see no. 59176, 54-55). In column 1 he states the number of goats in his charge; in columns 2 and 3 he gives a list of kids, milk, and cheese for which he has not yet been paid; and in column 4 he strikes a balance between the money due to him and the amount of the rent which he has to pay to Zenon. The balance in his favor is very small; but it must be remembered that we do not have a full account of the produce sold by him, and the balance of ten drachmae is not to be regarded as the whole of his profit. In column 2 certain persons are mentioned as purchasers of kids, milk, and cheeses: Athenagoras, Theophilos, and Eukles. These were probably not retailers, but wealthy men who bought supplies for their households. Athenagoras appears again in the *Italian Society Papyri* (P.S.I.), 353, 354 and may perhaps have been a high official in the Memphite district <term>nome: an administrative division or province of ancient Egypt</term>; Theophilos may be the person mentioned in *P.S.I.*, 513 and no. 59294; and Eukles was one of the prominent citizens of Philadelphia (see no. 59366).

### 59330. Letter from Pemnas to Zenon. — 0 m. 12 x 0 m. 27. — Date: 30th June, 248 B.C.

The writer, who was a swineherd (see no. 59292, throughout), complains to Zenon that Herakleides, arranging privately with Thoteus, has made up the account of the arrears of rent owed by the swineherds, without allowing him to go through the account and check it. He has already protested several times to Iason about their conduct. Herakleides too holds all the contracts made with the swineherds in his own hands.

The rent <note>original: "phoros"</note> mentioned in line 2 is not a Government tax, but the rent in kind which the native swineherds paid to Zenon or whoever owned the pigs. We possess a contract concerning the hire of a herd of goats (no. 59340; see also no. 59238),

<column-break/>

<page-num>53</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

and no doubt those concerning the pigs were of the same nature. Herakleides was the man who had charge of this business at Philadelphia; in *P.S.I.*, 384, he is described as "the one managing the pig-business" <note>original: "ten hyiken pragmateuomenos"</note>; and in *P.S.I.*, 379 and 381 we find him receiving young pigs as rent from the swineherds.

Pemnas to Zenon, greetings. Concerning the amounts owed by
the swineherds from previous times along with the rent of Year 37,
Herakleides, having come to an agreement with Thoteus, they themselves
settled the accounts without us, and we are not able to follow what they have done
5 until now; nor when asked for the account did they dare to give it to us.
And concerning these matters I have frequently protested to Iason that they
are not acting rightly in having come to this agreement. Herakleides also holds
all the contracts made with the swineherds. I have written to you then about
these things so that you may know.
->Farewell. Year 38, Pachon 10.<- <note>June 30, 248 B.C.</note>

### 59332. Letter from Korragos to Proxenos. — 0 m. 15 x 0 m. 345. — Date: summer of 248 B. C.

Korragos complains that in spite of an order given on the king's birthday he and his men have not yet received all the pay <note>original: "opsonion"; a term for military or official wages/rations</note> due to them. He blames Leukippos the scribe <note>original: "grammateus"</note> for this and asks Proxenos not to permit such conduct on the part of his subordinates.

If the words in line 2 mean ‘the salary which is given to those of us who go to Kanopos’ <note>A city near Alexandria, often visited for royal festivals</note>, we may infer that a party was sent every year to assist at the celebration of the king's birthday and the anniversary of his accession (see Wilcken, *Archiv*, VI, p. 395). The present text is one of those which show that the birthday fell in the month of Dystros.

Korragos appears again in some other papyri, in one of which we find him buying house property at Theadelphia and Pharbaitos for his sons Andromenes and Attalos. If he is identical with the Korragos "from Hermolaos" mentioned in another document, he must have been a Government employee in the Memphite or Aphroditopolite district; but the identification is not certain and the other texts yield no definite information about him. Nor does the reference to Proxenos in no. 59297, 22 enlighten us as to his position.

Korragos to Proxenos, greetings. Regarding the thirty-seventh year, [during the month of] Dystros [...]

*Line 1.* If this means ‘for the whole of year 37’, the explanation suggested above cannot be right. But as the new year began about the end of Dystros, the writer

<column-break/>

# ZENON PAPYRI

may be referring to a short period of service, part of which fell in year 37 and part in year 38. Dystros was probably followed by a date, "on the birthday [celebrations]" being added as an explanation.
&emsp; *Lines 2-3.* This might also mean ‘orders were given to pay those who were going to Kanopos, whereas my men etc.’, but the other explanation seems preferable.
&emsp; *Line 4.* ‘Who had been sent with a letter of introduction to Leukippos the scribe in order to receive from him the pay and the supplies’.
&emsp; *Line 5.* There is an empty space between "bound" <note>original: "dedemenon"</note> and "I sent for," as if the writer had meant to insert some such word as "having heard."
&emsp; *Line 7.* Compare other papyri: "until the twenty-sixth year and the month of Dystros." The meaning here is ‘for that part of Dystros which falls in year 38 and for the month of Xandikos’ and in the other case ‘up to the end of year 26, including the whole of Dystros’.

[Continuation of letter 59332]
on the birthday, the wage which is given to us who travel to Kanopos with the
[...]

### 59333. Account of wheat. — 1 m. 02 x 0 m. 17. — Date : May-July, 248 B. C.

Written on a long strip of papyrus, along the fibres, on the side which is really the back of the roll. It is an account of the wheat given out as food allowances to various members of Zenon's circle in the months of Pharmouthi and Pachons of year 38. ### 59334. Account of sows. — 0 m. 085 X 0 m. 195. — Date: August 5, 248 B.C.

An account from Herakleides (see no. 59330) concerning the sows owned by Zenon and leased to various individuals. On the back is a list showing the number of sows each swineherd currently possesses and how many are missing. The text is written along the fibers on the front, and only the top portion remains. It is dated "Pauni 16, in Alexandria," suggesting Zenon received the report while staying in the city.

# 59337. Letter from Iason to Zenon. — 0.13 m x 0.16 m and 0.12 m x 0.16 m. — Date: 2nd October, 248 B.C.

Iason writes that he has gone to Moithymis to see Leon about the land tax <note>original: "eparourion," a tax of 3 drachmae per aroura on vineyards and orchards</note>, of which five years’ payment at the rate of three drachmae per aroura <note>An aroura was a unit of area roughly equal to 0.6 acres</note> was being exacted for the vineyard and orchard. He had asked Leon to wait and not sell the wine until Iason had written to Zenon. So Leon had given him three days in which to settle. Metrodoros also had written to Hermolaos to stop the sale until Zenon had been written to.

Leon, who was threatening to sell the wine in order to recover the arrears of the ground tax, was a subordinate of Hermolaos the œconome <note>A financial administrator or provincial manager</note> (*P. S. I.*, 372). Rostovtzeff may be right in regarding Hermolaos as the Memphite œconome, for he is often mentioned in connection with localities in the south of the Memphite province. In no. 59236 he appears to be acting as Aphroditopolite œconome, but it is possible, as Rostovtzeff maintains, that this was a temporary charge. The vineyard was one of the properties near Meidoum in which Zenon had a direct or indirect interest.

The fragment containing lines 8-13 is in Florence and has been published in *P. S. I.*, 650. The original height of the letter was 33 centimeters.

<header>CATALOGUE OF THE CAIRO MUSEUM</header>

After the usual protocol the contract states that Iason has leased out for two years to Demetrios and Limnaios 144 goats at an annual rent of 216 six-months-old kids. The rent is to be paid half-yearly. If they deliver less than the specified number of kids, they must pay at once a penalty price of ten drachmæ per head; and at the end of the lease, if they fail to return the goats as they received them, they have to pay a certain sum for each one not accounted for. On the other hand, if Iason takes the herd from them before the agreed time, he must pay them a fine of a hundred drachmæ. After the usual penalty clause authorising Iason to make exaction in case of default come the names of two sureties and six witnesses.

*Line 4.* In *P. Michigan Inventory*, 3125 Demetrios is called an Aspendian <note>from Aspendos in Pamphylia</note> of the "settlers" <note>original: "tes epigones", descendants of military settlers</note> and Limnaios was his brother.

*Line 5.* of kids etc. <note>original: "eriphon ktl."</note>: corrected from the accusative case to the genitive.
*Line 7.* The space seems insufficient for [let them pay] <note>original: "apoteisatosan"</note>; perhaps simply [let them give] <note>original: "dotosan"</note>. Contrast the penalty price with that of no. 59328, 104.
*Line 8.* For example, [to take back the goats from them and lease them to someone else].
*Line 9.* if <note>original: "eam"</note>: "m" corrected from "n", so apparently not followed by "but" <note>original: "de"</note>; perhaps, as Grenfell suggested, a rare form of "if".

## 59341. (a) Petition to Apollonios from Theopropos; (b) letter from Neon to Damonikos; (c) and (d) drafts. — 0 m. 325 X 0 m. 26. — Date: 247 B.C. (plates VIII, IX).

(a) is written on the front of the papyrus, but is evidently a draft; the other three pieces are on the back. (b) is either the original letter or a good copy; its position on the back, the breadth of the papyrus and the absence of an address make the latter alternative the more probable. (c) and (d) are ordinary drafts in the hand of Zenon or his usual scribe.

<column-break/>

<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>
<page-num>67</page-num>

->(a)<-

Theopropos, who calls himself an <term>envoy</term> <note>theoros; a representative sent on a sacred or official mission</note> from Kalynda in Caria, states that his farmer Theron had obtained from that city a contract for supplying the wine used at the annual festival in Kypranda. Actually the wine was supplied on behalf of Theron by Theopropos himself, who had to borrow money to purchase it, and the sum due from the city for the supply of wine came to 850 drachmæ. The city treasurers, Diophantos and Akrisios, had repaid 600 drachmæ of this amount, but declined to pay the remaining 250, because the subscriptions had not all been paid up. On being summoned by Theopropos to appear before Motes the <term>governor</term> <note>strategos; a high-ranking military and administrative official</note> and Diodotos the <term>financial manager</term> <note>oeconomus; the official in charge of a district’s economy</note>, they pleaded that they could not pay without being authorized by a resolution of the assembly. The presiding officials <note>prytaneis</note> and the secretary <note>grammateus</note> procrastinated and had not yet proposed the resolution when Theopropos came to Egypt along with the treasurer Diophantos, the two having been elected by the city to act as <term>envoys</term> <note>theoroi</note>. He therefore asks Apollonios to write to the city and to the governor and the manager to see that the 250 drachmæ are repaid.
The governor and the manager mentioned here were no doubt royal officers who exercised a general control over the self-governing city or perhaps over a group of such cities. It is to be noted that in the present case, in which the king’s interests were not involved, they were content to let the matter follow its normal course. On the other hand Theopropos appeals to them as the superior authority, and it is clear that a message from Apollonios was regarded as the surest way of getting the assembly to pass the required resolution.
Theopropos came to Egypt as an <term>envoy</term> <note>theoros</note> in year 39. As the five-year festival <note>Pentaeteris</note> was due to be celebrated in the course of the autumn, his mission was probably to pay homage to the king on this particular occasion. Note the phrase <term>to the king</term> <note>original: pros ton basilea</note> as in *P. Freib.*, 7. The fact that the draft of his petition was found in Zenon’s files suggests that he had drawn it up in consultation with Zenon, who had a family connection with Kalynda, and that Zenon himself had come down to Alexandria for the festival.

->(b)<-

In this letter Neon, another citizen of Kalynda, asks Damonikos to speak to Zenon on his behalf. Neon’s father Therarchos, by an order from Alexandria (no doubt emanating from Apollonios the <term>chief finance minister</term> <note>dioiketes</note>), had been released from the obligation of providing quarters for soldiers or other employees of the State, as well as hay and pasture for the cavalry. When Therarchos died, the burden was reimposed upon Neon, who now asks for a new exemption to be written under his own name. He hopes to come to Egypt himself, but in the meantime urges his correspondent to plead his cause with Zenon and to engage the help of some of their friends.

->(c)<-

A draft of a memorandum on the same subject from Zenon (no doubt to Apollonios), in which he mentions that Therarchos had married an aunt of his. He asks Apollonios

### 59342. Letter from Sisouchos to Zenon. — 0.12 m X 0.145 m and 0.115 m X 0.165 m. — Date: 31st January, 246 B.C.

A repetition of a request to Zenon to write to the officials in Krokodilopolis <note>the capital of the Fayoum province</note> asking them to give a clerkship to Ptolemaios, probably the author's son. Sisouchos has sent the youth in person to see Zenon and begs him to write at once and get him appointed to a post with a fair salary.
The letter is dated year 39, month of Choiak, day 10, though it is probable that Ptolemy III had been king of Egypt for the last day or two and that it was now "Year 1." But it would naturally take some little time for the news of the old king's death to reach the villages in the Fayoum. For Sisouchos, see entry no. 59264.

Sisouchos to Zenon, greetings. [I have] previously written 
concerning Ptolemaios my [son, so] that you might send instructions to the circle of Hermaphilos 
and Python the ba[nker] to appoint him to a clerical post; 
I have [sent] Ptolemaios himself to you. If, therefore, it seems good to you...

*Line 1.* A phrase like "I know indeed" seems required in the gap.
*Line 2.* "son" is a conjecture, but is of the right length for the gap in the papyrus. The mention of Hermaphilos indicates that he had succeeded Aristandros as *oeconome* <note>district financial manager</note> of the Arsinoite province in the last year of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.
*Line 3.* "to a clerical post" : compare the phrase used by the historian Polybius, "the one appointed over the records."

<keywords>Zenon, Neon, billeting, cavalry tax, Calynda, Sisouchos, Ptolemaios, Krokodilopolis, clerkship, Ptolemy III, oeconomos, horse breeding</keywords>

### 59343. Letter from Spinther to Zenon. — 13 x 20.5 cm. — Date: 247 or 246 B.C.

The writer's language is ungrammatical and it is not easy to follow his meaning. Some Government agents had made a descent on the boat on which he was employed, demanding payment of the tax for year 39. Zenon is therefore requested to write and say what arrangement Petosiris is to make. Spinther adds that they have not yet received the pitch <note>used for waterproofing the hull</note> and that Rodippos was insisting that someone must render an account of this.

&emsp;&emsp;Spinther to Zenon, greetings. Know that we have managed the affairs regarding the boat's equipment <note>original: "skea," a misspelling of "skeue"</note>, having received letters for Memphis and for Hermopolis. Just as we were about to anchor, Alexander's men <note>Alexander was likely a local police chief or tax official</note> intercepted 5 us, saying that the tax for the 39th year <term>chiliagogos</term> <note>a tax on boats with a capacity of 1,000 artabae, roughly 30 tons</note> must be paid. You, therefore, write to us what arrangement Petosiris should make. Know also that we have not yet received the pitch; for which reason he <note>Petosiris?</note> did not sit still, but Rodippos said that he must render an account.
&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;Farewell.

10 **VERSO:**&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;To Zenon.

<note>Line 2. "skea": read "skeue" (equipment). — "eilephotes": read "eilephotas" (having received).</note>
<note>Line 3. "pp": read "de" (but/and).</note>
<note>Line 4. Alexander: possibly the chief of police or a tax-collector.</note>
<note>Line 5. "deitai": probably a mistake for "dei to telos" (the tax is required).</note>
<note>Line 7. "eilephotes": read "eilephotas".</note>

<page-num>78</page-num>
<header>CATALOGUE OF THE CAIRO MUSEUM.</header>

Assume that the letter comes from Zenon’s archives, though it does not bear his name. A certain Ariston had been accused by a swineherd of having stolen a pig at the time of the festival of Demeter. Philonichos summoned Neon, **commander** <note>original: "ἐπιστάτης" — a local official or overseer</note> of the cavalrymen at Bacchias, together with Ariston and some of the land-holding soldiers <note>original: "cleruchs" — soldiers granted land in exchange for service</note>, and held an inquiry. Ariston maintained that the pig which he had sacrificed was his own. The swineherd, he said, had come to his house during the festival and asked to have it searched, but on being told to wait until the women were removed he went off without doing anything more. Such was the result of the inquiry.

Philonichos to Eukles, greetings. Having received the letter from you, I summoned Neon the commander of the cavalry in Bacchias and some of the cavalrymen and Ariston, about whom you wrote to me to investigate regarding the sacrificial animal, and when questioned in the presence of the aforementioned, he stated that the sacrificial animal had not been stolen <note>original: "μὴ ὑβειρῆσθαι"</note>, but that he had sacrificed his own fattened pig, and he displayed the meat;
<margin>5</margin> and he said the swineherd arrived during the **fast of Demeter** <note>original: "νηστείαι τῆς Δήμητρος" — the second day of the Thesmophoria festival</note> and asked him for a search of the house, but he told him to wait until he had removed the womenfolk, and the swineherd, having heard this from Ariston, went away and left. I have therefore written to you so that you may know.
->Farewell. Year 3, Phaophi 5.<-

*Line 2. Ariston* : it is not clear whether this was Zenon’s colleague (see no. 59371) or merely one of the land-holding soldiers at Bacchias.
*Line 3.* The letters read as {ρει} may be a separate word, but I can make nothing else out of them.
*Line 5. fast* : this was the name of the second day of the **Thesmophoria** <note>A women-only festival in honor of Demeter and Persephone</note> in Athens, and the date of the letter corresponds with the time of year at which the Thesmophoria were held. The Ptolemaic festival was probably modeled on the Athenian. For another allusion to the **Demeter-festival** <note>original: "Δημήτρια"</note> see no. 59028. See too the fragment of Philikos published by Medea Norsa in *Stud. Ital. di Phil. clas.*, N. S., V, p. 90. Mr. Bell informs me that *Br. Mus. Invent.* 2654 contains a memorandum of work to be done on the temple of Demeter at Philadelphia.
*Line 6. search* : equivalent to "a search be conducted." — **removing the womenfolk** <note>original: "τὰ γύναια μεταστῆσαι"</note> : a similar embarrassment is caused by the *harem* at the present day, when a house is being searched for stolen goods. But Ariston’s womenfolk may have been engaged in some secret rites in connection with the festival.
*Line 8.* The date of the letter is probably a good many days later than the date of the festival.

### 59351. Petition from Zenon to the king. — 0 m. 07 x 0 m. 35. — Date : about 243 B. C. (pl. X).

A formal petition of the sort which, though addressed to the king, was often, perhaps usually, presented to the **strategos** <note>the military governor</note> of the district. For the latest discussion of this question see COLLOMP, *Recherches sur la chancellerie et la diplomatique des Lagides*. The present document, however, whether it be the original petition or a copy, has evidently not been used.
Zenon complains about a certain Herakleides to whom he had given 400 **drachmae** <note>Greek unit of currency</note> in gold to pay to the Treasury on his behalf 400 drachmae in copper, on condition that when Herakleides received the copper he would repay the gold. But though Zenon had been offering him the copper and demanding repayment of the gold, Herakleides had put him off up to the present. Zenon therefore asks the king to order Agenor the **strategos** to summon Herakleides and compel him to fulfil his bargain.
From no. 59022 we learn that a hundred drachmae in gold had an exchange value of at least a hundred and four drachmae in silver. And as 104 drachmae in silver at the ordinary rate of exchange were worth nearly 115 drachmae in copper, Zenon’s 400 drachmae in gold were probably worth about 460 in copper.

To King Ptolemy, greetings from Zenon. I am being wronged by Herakleides; for when I gave him in the 3rd year through Demeas 400 **gold drachmae** <note>symbolized by ⊢ υ</note>, so that he might pay on my behalf to the royal treasury 400 **copper drachmae**, on the condition that when he received them from me he would return [the gold] to me, and though I have been offering to pay him and demanding it back from him, he has not returned it, but has put me off until now. I therefore beg you, if it seems good to you, to command Agenor the **strategos** to summon him and, if these things are true, to compel him,
<margin>5</margin> upon receiving the 400 drachmae of copper, to return to me the 400 drachmae of gold, and so **through you I shall have obtained justice.** <note>original: "διὰ σὲ τοῦ δικαίου τετευχώς"</note>
->May you be fortunate.<-

*Line 1.* There is an empty space at the end of the line with traces of deleted letters.
*Line 5. and let me obtain* : ‘and let me obtain’. The same phrase occurs again without a preceding *so that* <note>original: "ἵνα"</note> in one of the Michigan papyri.

**BIBLIOGRAPHY** : *Museum Entry Journal*, no. 48799; *P. Edg.*, no. 58; *Zeitschrift für Numismatik* XXXIII, p. 73 (Schubart); *Sammelbuch*, 6764.

### 59355. Draft of a statement concerning a loan. — 0.35 m. x 0.565 m. — Date: summer of 243 B.C. (plate XII).

In 259 B.C., Zenon had lent some money to a certain Philon, probably the <term>baker</term> <note>original: "σιτοποιός" (sitopoios)</note> attached to Apollonios’ household. The debt had never been repaid in full and there had been a dispute about the amount still due. Philon had presented a complaint to a high official called Chrysermos, who had delegated two examining judges, Zenis and Diodoros, to hear the case and report to him. These judges had decided (1) that Zenon should present his account against Philon in accordance with the facts both parties admitted and (2) that with regard to their mutual accusations they should exchange pledges in the temple of Sarapis. The latter instruction had been complied with, and our papyrus is a long and complicated draft of the statement which Zenon had been ordered to hand in. In the four columns of the front side (recto) he gives a detailed account of the money due to him from Philon and ends with a memorandum to the arbitrators asking them to report to Chrysermos without delay and let him return to his fields and vineyards. The first column of the back side (verso) contains a re-draft of a paragraph from the front; then a draft beginning *Regarding Philon*, perhaps intended as a general heading; and then a re-draft of the memorandum to the arbitrators. Below is an abbreviated statement of the account, drawn up on a different basis. It breaks off at line 154 of column 2. At line 155 begins a third statement, similar in general to the first statement, but more summary, less carefully drawn up, and incomplete.

The amount of the loan according to the first and third statements was 900 drachmae in silver, and the rate of interest was 2 per cent a month, payable in copper, which on the Macedonian calendar with its system of every-two-years addition of a month (intercalation) makes 25 per cent a year. From the beginning of year 28 to the middle of year 29 the salary due to Philon as an employee of Apollonios was intercepted by Zenon and applied in the first place to paying the interest on the loan and in the second place to paying off the principal (capital). In year 29, about the time when Zenon retired to the <term>countryside</term> <note>original: "χώρα" (chora) — the Egyptian interior outside of Alexandria</note>, this method of payment ceases, perhaps, as the historian Rostovtzeff suggests, because he had no longer control of the salary. The debt was further reduced by the transfer of two female slaves from Philon to Zenon, their value—or more probably a third of their value—being deducted from the amount still owing and the deduction being allowed to take effect from the middle of year 29. Thus by the end of the month of Dios in that year, Philon had reduced his debt to 505 drachmae, 5 obols, interest paid up to date. For the next 12 1/2 years the interest on this sum would have amounted to 1500 drachmae; but the principle that interest on a loan must not accumulate beyond the amount of the principal is now applied, and the interest on the loan in question is reduced to 505 drachmae, 5 obols, in copper. During the same period (see columns 3 and 4) Zenon had various other transactions with Philon, with the result that the latter finally owes him 647 drachmae, 3 obols, in silver, together with the interest just mentioned.

The *second statement* (lines 133-154) seems to have been drafted as an alternative proposal, but as it breaks off in the middle, Zenon probably decided to drop it and return to the first calculation. In this second statement the amount of the loan appears as 410 drachmae, bearing the usual interest of 2 per cent per month, while a further sum of 10 drachmae is paid monthly under the title of *apophora* <note>original: "ἀποφορά" — a payment made by a slave or an employee to their master/employer from their earnings</note>. The general meaning of this seems to be that certain slaves employed by Philon are regarded as Zenon's property, hired out to Philon at so much per month. The account probably breaks off at the point of time when the elder of the two slaves mentioned above had been transferred to Zenon's household, after which the *apophora* would be paid on the second slave only until the time of her transfer. The way in which the loan and the question of ownership are mixed up and the hypothesis in the second statement that Zenon was the owner of the two slaves from the beginning suggest that Philon had borrowed the money in order to buy slaves from Zenon. But with such details as we have it seems scarcely possible to arrive at a satisfactory explanation of the whole business.

The handwriting of the draft is not all of one character, whether various scribes were employed on it or whether it was written by the same person but with varying degrees of carefulness. The four columns of the recto <note>the "front" or smooth side of the papyrus</note> are in a clear, upright hand. But lines 20, 31, 68-70, 93-97, 100-103 have been sponged out and rewritten in a thicker and more formal hand, while some of the corrections above the lines have been added at the same time. The verso <note>the "back" of the papyrus</note> up to line 154 is in a more cursive hand (that of Zenon or his usual clerk, compare number 59129), and the remainder of the last column is still more cursive. Words, phrases and whole lines are cancelled sometimes by a line drawn through them, sometimes by being enclosed in round brackets, but in my transcription all these deletions are indicated without distinction by double square brackets [[ ]].

*Line 102. pledges* <note>original: "πίστεις"</note>: the meaning is that they assured each other on oath that they withdrew their mutual allegations.
*Lines 102-103. the Sarapieion of Parmeniskos*: Wilcken has pointed out that this must be the great Sarapieion in Alexandria of which Parmenion, popularly called Parmeniskos, was the architect. It follows from this observation that the trial took place in Alexandria, where Philon seems to have been domiciled.
*Lines 104-105. from agreed facts* <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν ὁμολόγων"</note>: according to what was admitted by both parties.
*Line 106.* "having judged" corrected to "you judged."
*Line 107. Chrysermos*: probably the Chrysermos mentioned by the historian Plutarch in *Cleomenes*, 36, 1. His name appears several times in the papyri; he is mentioned as the owner of a large estate <term>dorea: a gift of land from the king to a high official</term>. Lesquier proposes to identify the owner of the estate with the Chrysermos entitled "Kinsman of King Ptolemy and Exegetes and in charge of the Physicians and President of the Museum" in a known inscription; and in spite of the observations of Dittenberger the identification seems to me now to be quite possible. But we cannot yet say in what capacity Chrysermos was acting in the present case.

### 59357. Letter of Demetrios to Zenon. — 0.345 m X 0.085 m. — Date: 4th November, 243 B.C.

Demetrios, a farmer of the <term>apomoira: a tax of one-sixth of the produce of vineyards and orchards, dedicated to the cult of the goddess-queen Arsinoe Philadelphos</term> (see no. 59367), tells Zenon, who seems to have had a financial interest in the farm, that he has sent him the accounts of the proceeds of the vineyards in the <note>administrative districts</note> of Themistes and Polemon, but that he has not yet received the accounts of the rest of the <term>nome: a provincial district of Egypt</term> from his assistants. He asks him after going through the accounts to send them back in order that he may complete them. He has already sold the wine in Kersesoucha at six drachmae and the <note>original: "ὄξος" (oxos), sour wine or vinegar</note> at two and a half.

### 59358. Fragment of letter to Zenon. — 0.21 m x 0.14 m. — Date: 1st February, 242 B.C.

The fragment mentions the birthday of the king and queen and speaks of providing wine and sacrificial pigs for the festival. The birthday of the king fell on the 5th of Dios and the anniversary of his accession on the 25th; the birthday of the queen is supposed to have been the 9th of some month, perhaps Dios (see DITTENBERGER, *O. G. I. S.*, 56, 34, note), but possibly the two birthdays were celebrated together. It is not clear, however, whether the "festival" <note>original: ἑορτή</note> of line 6 is the birthday feast or that of the accession. The latest evidence makes it probable that in year 4 Choiak 12 corresponded approximately to Dios 15; but our information about the Macedonian calendar in the reign of Euergetes <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes</note> is still very defective and contradictory.

### 59359. Letter from Antipatros to Zenon. — 0.32 m x 0.11 m. — Date: 14th June, 242 B.C.

Put together out of four fragments acquired at different times. Antipatros requests Zenon to get the letter from Sostratos about the garden, in order that he may come to terms and have money for harvesting the poppy crop. He had not been able previously to come to terms with Menelaos' people owing to his sudden departure. The business about which he went down to Alexandria is proceeding favourably, though he was not able to bring it to a conclusion, as Zenodoros (see no. 59368) had no time to attend to him; he feels sure, however, that it will be settled in Memphis.

### 59361. Account sent by Demetrios to Kriton. — 0.175 m. x 0.415 m. — Date: 25th July, 242 B.C.

Demetrios, one of the farmers of the *apomoira* <note>A 1/6th tax on the produce of vineyards and orchards, originally dedicated to the cult of the deified Queen Arsinoe Philadelphus</note> in the Arsinoite district <term>nome</term>, sends Kriton, who like Zenon probably had a financial interest in the tax farm, a copy of the settlements which he has made for certain districts. The account was written in the middle of summer, and the sums mentioned in it seem to be the assessed yield of the tax in various localities. In most cases the settlement is made "by agreement with" <note>original: πρὸς</note> specific people, and sometimes it is noted that the amount was previously a certain sum "by direct management" <note>original: ἐξ αὐτουργίας</note>. The meaning of these phrases is not entirely certain; but perhaps *by agreement with* <note>original: πρὸς</note> indicates a deal made with local delegates of the Government, while *previously by direct management* <note>original: πρότερον ἐξ αὐτουργίας</note> indicates a previous estimate made by the tax farmers themselves. This would align with the regulations in the *Revenue Laws*, column 28, regarding the tax on fruit, though not with what we know about the procedure for the wine tax.

->Column I.<-

->Demetrios to Kriton, greetings.<-
->Jason is bringing the copies<-
->of the administration that has taken place<-
---
->From the Polemon district <term>meris</term><-
<margin>5</margin> ->excluding the thousand-aroura <note>An 'aroura' is a Greek unit of land measurement</note> vineyard near the<-
->Island of the Guards <note>original: Phylakitike Nesos</note><-
->31,000 and 2,000 silver drachmae <note>The symbol ト denotes silver drachmae</note><-
->by agreement with Orses and Hegemon.<-
->As for the thousand-aroura vineyard, we estimate it<-
<margin>10</margin> ->at the reduced sum of 1,000 silver drachmae<-
->for which it will be necessary to send reliable guards<-
->from our side / Total: 31,000 and 3,000 silver drachmae<-

<column-break/>

->Column II.<-

->City of Leto <note>original: Λητοῦς πόλις</note>: previously it<-
->was 2,000, but now by agreement with Theophilos<-
<margin>15</margin> ->and Petalos: 2,600 silver drachmae<-

Lines 2-3. The word *we have sent* <note>original: ἀπεστάλκαμεν</note> is omitted or is to be understood.
Lines 9-10. "We assess at the reduced sum of 1,000 drachmae."
Line 13. *City of Leto* <note>original: Λητοῦς πόλις</note>: this and the other places mentioned in the same column were in the Herakleides district <term>meris</term>. See *P. Teb.*, II, Appendix, where all of them are noted with the exception of Teschitis.

**59362. Front side <note>original: Recto</note>: letter to Zenon. Back side <note>original: Verso</note>: a receipt from Zenon to Pyrrhos. —**
0.39 m. X 0.115 m. — Date: 5th November, 242 B.C. (plate XIII).

The writer had received a letter from Zenon ordering him to keep faith with certain shepherds (see *flocks* <note>original: ποίμνια</note> in line 4), who were dissatisfied with the land assigned to them for pasturage. In answer, he protests that he has not only given them the place which they had leased, but another piece as well, for which he might have received a price from other people. But they insisted on him giving them some land which he had already disposed of by contract and which was scattered through various irrigation basins. This he refused to cede, but in accordance with Zenon’s request, he gave them 200 *arourai* <note>a unit of land measurement approximately 2/3 of an acre</note> of dry land in one basin. In the postscript, he asks for some goads for guarding the wild oxen.

In the duplicate receipt on the back side, Zenon acknowledges that he has received from Pyrrhos the rent for the pigs which the latter, in partnership with Pytheas, had hired from Epharmostos (Zenon’s brother) according to a contract deposited with Archagathos. The amount was 50 drachmae, and also the pigs themselves numbering 12 1/2 (representing Pyrrhos’ share of a total of 25). The text is either a draft or, more probably, was not used because of the writing on the front. The note at the end refers to a previous receipt and recalls the phrase found on pottery fragments <note>original: ostraca</note>: “do not use the one written previously” <note>original: τῶι δὲ πρότερον γραφέντι μὴ χρήσηι; Wilcken, *Ostr.*, I, p. 78; Milne, *Theban Ostr.*, no. 16</note>. The scholar Wilcken <note>original: *Archiv*, VII, p. 77</note> takes "the former letter" <note>original: τῆι προτέραι ἐπιστολῆι</note> to mean the first of the two drafts; but if this is right, the instruction has little point, as the two are exactly alike.

> [... to Zeno]n, greetings. You wrote
> [...] Demetrios
> [      to th]em I had given
> [            ]other flocks <note>original: ποίμνια</note>
> <margin>5</margin> [            ] nothing true.

<note>Line 1. As the writer must have had a short name of four or five letters, he may possibly have been Damis, who in another papyrus informs Zenon “I also arranged the pasture for the Arabs, just as you wrote to me, though others already held it.” But as the present text is eight years later, the attribution is very doubtful.</note>
<note>Line 2. Demetrios: It has been suggested that this may have been the commander of ten <note>original: dekadarch</note> of the Arabs mentioned in other documents. There is something to be said for the identification, but it is far from certain.</note>

### 59363. Letter from Philinos to Zenon. — 0.275 m x 0.10 m. — Date:
### 26th November, 242 B.C.

An urgent request to Zenon to send the wheat and the barley and also a <term>sitometres</term> <note>A <term>sitometres</term> was a professional grain-measurer responsible for certifying the quantity of grain during transactions.</note> to effect the proper delivery of them. Prices are falling every day, sometimes by half an obol, sometimes a quarter.

We possess many letters from Philinos. Rostovtzeff identifies him as a military commander who likely owned a <term>dorea</term> <note>A <term>dorea</term> was a large estate granted by the king to high-ranking officials.</note>. It is certain he was a neighbor of Zenon for many years and on very friendly terms with him. In another letter, he even invites Zenon and his brothers to a great banquet.
