## 59366. Statement concerning money owed by a surety. — 0 m. 175 x 0 m. 108. — Date: about 241 B. C. (pl. XI).

Demeas, one of Zenon's friends (see Index V), had made himself surety <note>A surety is someone who takes legal responsibility for another person's debt.</note> for the potter Horos, who had undertaken the provision of pottery for year 4 to the district which had once formed the estate of Apollonios. Horos having failed to fulfil his contract, Demeas had become responsible for the deficit to Bion, who had lately succeeded Eukles as <term>epistates</term> <note>original: ἐπιστάτης; a district administrator or overseer.</note>. The deficit was 2700 jars, the value of which was 270 drachmæ. Whether the text was a receipt for this sum or an acknowledgment of the claim is not certain. Perhaps the most interesting point in it is the reference to the estate, "formerly belonging to Apollonios" <note>original: τῆς πρότερον οὔσης Ἀπολλωνίου</note>, which shows that Apollonios was now either dead or in disgrace. Zenon, however, still continued to live in Philadelphia, devoting his time to his own private affairs.

The verso <note>The back side of the papyrus.</note>, which has no connection with the recto <note>The front side of the papyrus.</note>, contains a note of certain sums paid or payable by Zenon.

> In Philadelphia, of the estate formerly
> belonging to Apollonios,
> on behalf of Demeas son of Kal... <note>original: Καλ..[..; likely Kallias</note> [for]
> the surety which Demeas guaranteed 
> 5 to Eukles son of Dionysios, [overseer of the...]
> at Philadelphia, the estate having been
> reclaimed <note>original: ἀναληφθείσης; meaning the land was taken back by the crown.</note> after [the death?]
> of Apollonios, [to] Horos [the] Naucratite
> potter, who had taken
> 10 over from Eukles [in the 3rd year?]
> the pottery contract for the 4th year [according to]
> the agreement, for which [Zenon was]
> the contract-keeper <note>original: συγγραφοφύλαξ; a third party who held the legal documents.</note>, the portion falling to Demeas
> from what Horos additionally owed to Eukles
> 15 for jars, which he [delivered or credited]...

<margin>
*Line 3.* Kallias is the most probable name.
*Line 5.* Possibly "overseer of the...", but the traces of letters do not accord very well with this reading.
*Lines 6-7.* "having been reclaimed": restored by Grenfell.
*Line 10.* Perhaps "in the 3rd year".
*Line 11.* Horos had evidently contracted to supply a certain number of jars required for wine in the district of Eukles.
*Line 12.* "contract-keeper" is probable.

## 59367. Drafts of letters from Zenon to various persons. — 0 m. 30 x 0 m. 225. — Date: 20th January, 240 B. C. (pl. XIV).

The first letter is addressed to Sostratos. Demetrios, who was engaged in farming the <term>apomoira</term> <note>original: ἀπόμοιρα; a tax on the produce of vineyards and orchards, traditionally one-sixth.</note> had lately sailed down to see Zenodoros and ask that an order should be sent to Hermaphilos the <term>oeconome</term> <note>A financial manager or steward.</note> and to the accountants to make inquiry and, if it should appear that the arrears of year 4 were covered by the surplus of year 5, to give back their bails to the sureties. Zenon had already written to Sostratos, when Demetrios was starting, to ask Kraton the <term>praktor</term> <note>A debt collector or official responsible for enforcing payments.</note> to deal indulgently with Dionysodoros in the matter of the 3000 drachmæ for which he guaranteed the firm of Hippokrates and Demetrios. Now it appeared that Zenodoros had sailed up to Sebennytos and that Demetrios had probably not found him in Alexandria.

<summary>This page documents a financial settlement involving a defaulted pottery contract and subsequent debt obligations for Zenon’s associates. It also reflects a major shift in the estate's status following the departure of Apollonios from power.</summary>
<keywords>Zenon, Demeas, Horos, Bion, Eukles, Philadelphia, Apollonios, pottery, drachma, arourai, vineyard tax, apomoira, epistates, oeconome, praktor, Alexandria</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the administrative and financial records of the Zenon Archive. Following the settlement of pottery debts in Philadelphia, these drafts concern complex tax-farming negotiations and labor disputes involving the estate’s partners and contractors.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
<header>CATALOGUE OF THE CAIRO MUSEUM.</header>

So if Sostratos has not already spoken to Kraton and obtained his consent, he is urged to do so without delay; otherwise, if the guarantee be exacted while the arrears are being made good, they are likely to lose 3000 drachmae; for it is not easy to recover anything from the Treasury.
The text seems to me to imply that, whoever was the nominal owner of the farm, Zenon and his partners had a financial interest in it, Hippokrates and Demetrios being the acting managers. If Dionysodoros was sold up and the arrears were afterwards made good, the loss might fall upon the farm, if the Treasury refused to refund the money already exacted. Compare *P. Gurob.*, 7, introduction. But the text is not explicit and the relations of the various parties are not very clear.
The second letter, of which we have only the opening lines, is addressed to Kraton and deals with the same subject.
The third draft, addressed to Sostratos, is about Samoelis and Alexandros, two Jews who had contracted to exploit the vineyard of Zenon and Sostratos (cf. no. 59269). The text is fragmentary and restoration is dubious; but apparently the contractors were complaining that they were prevented from passing through the neighbouring properties to obtain the reeds which they needed for training the vines. The robbery reported by them in *P. S. I.*, 393 seems to have taken place later. Zenon is alarmed at the idea that they may leave the vineyard and renounce their contract, and he asks Sostratos to take some steps in order to prevent this.
Below is a fragment of another letter to the two vine-dressers about the same matter.

Line 9. *you may take care* : wrongly transcribed as *epimeleses* in the first edition (see *Mayser, Gramm.*, II, p. 116).
Line 10. *the 3000 drachmae* : though Grenfell doubted this reading, preferring 50 drachmae and suggesting a different symbol in line 19, I still think that my transcription is right.
Line 17. *having done [this]* : as if preceded by "it would be well if you did this."
Line 19. Zenon has hesitated between two forms of the word for "suffer loss." The meaning, as the words stand, seems to be : ‘lest a premature exaction from Dionysodoros cause us to lose 3000 drachmae’. That is, they would have to repay Dionysodoros and run the risk of recovering nothing from the Treasury.
Line 21. — *os* and — *es* corrected from — *ou* and — *en*. Read *those who became* accordingly.
Line 27. Perhaps *passing through [the estates]*; see lines 32-33.

# 59368. Letter from Sostratos to Zenon and Xenophon. — 0 m. 325 x 0 m. 265. — Date: 26th July, 240 B.C.

Sostratos writes that he is sending a copy of the letter which Sosibios has written to Zenodoros about the bee-hives and other matters and also a copy of the memorandum which he and Kleon had presented to Sosibios. If Ammonios is still refractory <note>meaning stubborn or unmanageable</note>, he asks his correspondents to send him the bee-keepers and Rhodon with all the justificatory documents, in order that the case may be tried in his own district. Below is the letter of Sosibios, sending Zenodoros a copy of the memorandum and requesting him to see that the petitioners obtain justice.

Below this again is the memorandum from Kleon and Sostratos. They state that they own a thousand bee-hives leased to various natives, some in the Herakleopolite and some in the Memphite <term>nome</term><note>A "nome" was an administrative district or province in ancient Egypt.</note>. The latter hives had lately been transferred to the Herakleopolite nome without their permission and Ammonios the <term>oeconome</term><note>An oeconomus was a local financial administrator or "steward" of a district.</note> had imprisoned the bee-keepers, doing much damage to the hives, though afterwards, on the intervention of Sostratos and through fear of Zenodoros, he had released the prisoners. Again, he had arrested Rhodon, the guard of the petitioners' hay, and in the absence of the guard most of the hay was carried off by the natives; and though he had promised to recover the price of it, he had not yet done so. Moreover, the petitioners had hired a boat to carry the hay to Alexandria; owing to obstruction on the part of Ammonios' agents the boat had gone away empty; but all the same the owner claimed payment for hire. They therefore ask Sosibios to write to Ammonios to send the bee-keepers together with his own representative to the place where the petitioners are living, in order that the case may be tried there.

The official who was to examine the case, or to see that it was fairly examined, was Zenodoros. This is the same official who in no. 59367 is asked to give an order to the Arsinoite oeconome about a question of finance; in the same text we find him travelling from Alexandria to Sebennytos, while in no. 59359 he appears to be busy in Alexandria. From the scope of his authority we may conclude that he was either the <term>chief dioiketes</term> or a <term>hypodioiketes</term><note>A "dioiketes" was the finance minister of all Egypt; a "hypodioiketes" was his deputy or a regional director.</note>. The other texts suggest the higher post; but in the present case, as Jouguet and Collart have pointed out (*Lumbroso Collection*, p. 127), the fact that the memorandum was presented to Sosibios and forwarded by him to Zenodoros for necessary action rather indicates that the former held the superior position. They therefore, in agreement with Rostovtzeff, regard Sosibios as the dioiketes and Zenodoros as the hypodioiketes and suggest, as I too had done, that Sosibios may be identical with the famous minister of Ptolemy Philopator. The argument is certainly plausible.

The case, being one in which an oeconome was implicated, probably came under the jurisdiction of the dioiketes. We do not learn where Kleon and Sostratos were domiciled, but it seems to have been somewhere down the river, perhaps at Memphis. Another letter, written a week later (*P.S.I.*, 524), tells us that the messenger had failed to deliver the letter of Sosibios to Zenodoros. It is probable that Sosibios had replied to the petitioners, sending them a copy of his letter; for how [the text continues on the next page].

15 were in the <term>Herakleopolite district</term><note>The Herakleopolite nome, an administrative region in Middle Egypt</note>, for which the taxes were paid regularly until Year 6; others were in the <term>Memphite district</term><note>The region around the ancient capital of Memphis</note>, which Papes and Amenneus held. > *a.* The "former administration of Simaristos" seems to have been in the Oxyrynchite district, but it is difficult to suppose the contract was drawn up there. Perhaps that administration included part of the Herakleopolite district as well.
> *Line 19. Because of this:* The Greek *dia to* is used here as a causal link to the following complaint.
> *Line 20. juice extraction:* Rostowzew's previous note on this word was a misunderstanding; it refers to processing plant products.
> *Lines 22-23.* "Abroad with the king" refers to the military campaigns in Syria.
> *Line 24. 40 [loads]:* The usual unit for hay was a "bundle" (*desme*), twenty of which made a "load" (*phortion*). The writer likely means 40 loads.
> *Line 26. official inquiry:* This refers to a standard legal process in Ptolemaic law.
> *Line 28. Kriton:* Possibly a former naval commander (*stolarches*) turned private ship-owner.
> *Line 31.* Read *epeide* (since).

### 59369. Letter from Philemon to Zenon. — 0 m. 12 $\times$ 0 m. 29. — Date: August-September, 240 B.C. (plate X).

Philemon had a dispute with his father-in-law Herakleides about their shares in an orchard and the case had been brought before the <term>strategos</term><note>A high-ranking provincial governor and military commander</note> of the Arsinoite <term>nome</term><note>A district or administrative division in ancient Egypt</note>. But instead of speaking about the orchard, Herakleides had accused his opponent of being a household slave, and Zenon had been appealed to. Philemon therefore begs Zenon to write to Agenor the strategos to liberate him and let him return to his work.
The text is interesting from the legal point of view, but I do not venture to make any comment on it while the reading of line 4 is still so uncertain.

### 59371. Letter from Ariston to Zenon. — 0 m. 185 $\times$ 0 m. 085. — Date: 29th March, 239 B.C.

Ariston announces that on the 8th of <term>Mecheir</term><note>The sixth month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly February-March</note> Ammonios began to put the farms up to auction and that the baths are being leased without any deductions. He has therefore thought it best not to bid until Zenon comes and considers what they should offer.
Ammonios may possibly be the <term>oeconome</term><note>original: oikonomos; a financial manager of a district</note> of no. 59368. An Ariston is mentioned in no. 59052 and no. 59341 as a member of Zenon's circle or family, but I cannot say whether the present Ariston was the same person. In addition to the baths which Zenon owned privately (P. S. I., 377 and 584), it appears from this letter that he was also a farmer of Government baths. So at least I interpret these passages in accordance with the view of Grenfell and Hunt (*Papyri Hibeh*, 108 and 116).

**59374. Order about the delivery of a slave to her owner.** — 0 m. 175 $\times$ 0 m. 10. — Date: Year 16 (plate XI).

An order to deliver a Carian slave called Sappho, who was being sent down the river in a royal galley, into the custody of her owner Philammon, belonging to the troop of Nikophilos.
I doubt very much whether this papyrus really comes from the archives of Zenon. It is dated year 16, <term>Panemos embolimos</term> <note>A Macedonian month; "embolimos" means it was an intercalary or "leap" month added to the calendar to keep it in sync with the seasons.</note>. Now a lately recovered text proves that the intercalary month in the early years of Euergetes was Hyperberetaios, the last complete month of the regnal year, and it is not likely that the system was changed until the next reign. We need more evidence before we can hope to explain the present date, on which Ernst Meyer has unwisely based his reconstruction of the calendar in the reign of Euergetes.

->Year 16, intercalary Panemos.<-
->Release from the voyage downriver in a royal [galley]<-

### 59375. Letter from Addaios to Zenon. — 0 m. 20 X 0 m. 095 and 0 m. 20 X 0 m. 23.

Addaios, an agent of Apollonios at Memphis, is often mentioned in the documents of years 28 and 29. In the present letter he writes to Zenon about various matters. First of all he speaks about a fatted fowl which Zenon had asked for. He next complains that the tax-farmers or toll-collectors had confiscated some wine which he had been selling and that they refused to give it back in spite of the intercession of Apollonios, brother of Pythangelos; and he asks Zenon to intercede himself with the higher authorities. He then asks for an order to be sent, perhaps about the delivery of a certain article, and he begs Zenon not to forget to have purchases made for him of some other material of which he is running short. With regard to the oil, Zenon is requested to seal the <term>symbolon</term> <note>a receipt or customs pass</note> for Zopyros in order that the tax-collectors may allow him to carry it down the river; otherwise Addaios will be obliged to buy some oil at a higher price. Lastly he asks for an answer to the questions he has put in the letters which Zopyros is bringing.
Several passages in the text are obscure, partly owing to the gaps in the papyrus <note>original: "lacunæ"</note> but partly also to our ignorance of the circumstances. Though it probably dates from year 28 or 29, it seems to have been written at a time when Zenon was up the river or in the Fayoum (see "bring down the river" <note>original: "καταγάγηι"</note> in line 11).

Addaios to Zenon, greetings. You wrote to us [asking] that the fatted bird be sent to you. I therefore asked [....................................................]...boros the one who fattens

### 59376. Account of barley and money, from Aischines to Zenon. — 0.33 m x 0.095 m.

The first part of the text is an account of barley for the horses. It was measured by the "expenditure" standard, in which the <term>artab</term> <note>a Persian-derived dry measure, roughly 30–40 liters depending on the local standard</note> contained forty <term>choinikes</term> <note>a daily ration of grain, roughly 1 liter</note>. The horses had two feeds a day, and the allowance for each meal was thirteen choinikes for a horse and twelve for a mule. At the end is a short account of money given to the grooms for wages.

> Account from Aischines
> to Zenon regarding the
> barley of the 10 artabs. For
> two days, the total comes to five half-
> 5 artabs and four choinikes,
> and breakfast on the third day:
> half an artab and six choinikes,
> and for the mule, three half-artabs
> and one half-artab,
> 10 when the grey horse remained
> here, which Aristomachus 
> took when he departed; the remainder is with
> me and from the third day I am
> spending it on the two horses
> 15 for their evening meal.

<margin>Line 7. half-artab <note>original: "ἥμυσυ"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Line 11. Aristomachos: see P.S.I., 371, 17.</margin>

> 1 drachma — | the remainder is 6 —

### 59377. Memorandum to Zenon from Alexandros and Ismaelos. — 0.14 m x 0.175 m.

A complaint from two farmers, whose names <note>Alexander and Ishmael</note> proclaim them to be Jews, that some land which they were cultivating on contract had gone dry through Zenon’s failure to provide what was specified in the contract. As they had no crop last year and the land had suffered, they ask for an immediate loan to enable them to carry on.

> Memorandum to Zenon from Alexandros and
> Ismaelos. We petition you, since last year, when we 
> worked 3 ½ <term>aruras</term> <note>a measure of land, roughly 0.6 acres</note>, it happens that 
> while we worked those, an even larger area 
> 5 has become dry waste land because you did not supply 
> what was required by the contract; — so now we petition you to do 
> as you promised, and also to grant us a loan in advance; 
> for you yourself know that no crop was produced 
> because of the lack of water, and for the 
> 10 coming season, the land has suffered. Now therefore, 
> declare to us whatever seems best to you, so that we are not ruined.

<margin>Lines 2-7. The grammar is confused, but the meaning is fairly clear. The writers had undertaken the cultivation of a small portion of the estate on contract, their profits to come out of the crop.</margin>
<margin>Line 10. suffered <note>original: "πεπόνηκεν"</note>: referring to the soil/land.</margin>

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Museum Entry Journal*, no. 48904.

## 59387. Fragment of a letter from Apollonios. — 0.28 m x 0.195 m.

Apollonios speaks, apparently in a tone of dissatisfaction, about the clearing of part of his estate for cultivation, says that he has written to Zoilos (the <term>oikonomos: a high-ranking official in charge of the regional economy</term> at Krokodilopolis) to send surveyors to measure it up, and orders Panakestor to sow the land and see that none of it is left uncultivated. The gist of lines 1-11 seems to be that he is displeased to find that so much land needs once more to be cleared of brushwood in spite of the money already spent on it.

## 59388. Letter from Apollonios to Zenon. — 0.24 m x 0.165 m (plate XV).

An interesting but mutilated letter, in which Apollonios apparently gave instructions about the lengthening and widening of a canal between Philadelphia and the lake <note>likely Lake Moeris</note>. It seems probable from the text that the work was to be conducted through his agents and at his expense. But the length of the lines is uncertain and restoration is hazardous.

Apollonios to Zenon, greetings. [Write to us]...
...the canal... fish... <note>perhaps "the canal leading to the fish-pond"</note>...
...and you will be able [to complete] the remainder...
...for I wish it [to be led as far as]...
<margin>5</margin> [the] lake. And give orders also to the [architect]...
...to measure how many <term>stadia: a unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</term> [it is]...
...as far as the lake. And write [also whether the]...
[width] of the canal from the [bank]...
is less than [so many] <term>pecheis: cubits, approx. 45-50 cm</term>. For I wish...
<margin>10</margin> [having] calculated the expense...
[and] to make it wider.
->Farewell.<-

VERSO:

->To Zenon.<-

*Lines 2-3. For example:* [so that] the canal, which leads to the fish [pond, will be dry].
*Lines 3-4. For example:* [to work on] the remainder.
*Line 4. For example:* [to lead] it [as far as].
*Lines 5-6. Perhaps* to [the architect].
*Line 8. For example:* from the [bank].
*Lines 9-10. For example:* for I wish [to know]... [if it is possible].

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Museum Entry Journal*, no. 48916; *Edgar Papyri*, no. 101, introduction (cancel); *Catalogue of the Museum*, no. 59298.

### 59392. Letter from Apollonios to Apollodoros. — 0.07 m x 0.22 m.

The writer, to judge by the handwriting, does not seem to be the <term>dioiketes</term>, and it is even doubtful whether the papyrus comes from Zenon's archives. When acquired, the letter was still sealed, as if it had never been opened. The seal bore a faint image of a human bust facing forward. Apollonios informs Apollodoros that he has sent Harphaesis, the bearer of the letter, to Hermopolis and asks him to ensure he is not delayed by the officials at the toll-station. It is unclear which Hermopolis or which <term>phylake: a guard post or customs station</term> is intended.

->Apollonios to Apollodoros, greetings. We have sent<-
->Harphaesis, the bearer of this letter to you, to Hermopolis.<-
->Therefore, let it be your concern that he is not hindered by those at<-
->the guard station.<-

Verso:

->5 To Apollodoros.<-

<note>Line 3. The use of "in order that" <note>original: "hopos an"</note> is a linguistic marker; the dioiketes usually writes "hopos" without the particle "an."</note>

<meta>Bibl. : Journal d’entrée du Musée, no. 48922.</meta>

### 59393. Letter from Apollonios to Zenon. — 0.11 m x 0.11 m.

This letter is not from the <term>dioiketes: the chief financial officer of Egypt</term>, but from an Apollonios of a humbler position. He informs Zenon that he has been approached by a potential buyer for "the big horse," but he cannot negotiate the price until he knows Zenon’s asking price. ### 59394. Memorandum to Zenon from Apollonios. — 0.30 m x 0.21 m.

Written across the fibers and folded vertically. This memorandum provides an account of the dues payable on sheep and goats in the district of Philadelphia. This is likely the <term>ennómion: a pasturage tax</term>, though the term is not explicitly used in the text. Apollonios, who appears to be acting as an overseer, lists various flocks owned by private individuals (including Zenon), as well as <term>hierà próbata: temple sheep</term> and <term>basilikà próbata: royal or crown sheep</term>. He records the monetary amounts due for each category. 

One specific category is <term>laïkà próbata: sheep owned by native peasants</term>. Apollonios reports that he has collected a portion of these dues and used the money for various payments (lines 24–32), while the rest must still be collected from the individuals named in lines 34–53. It appears Zenon was responsible for collecting the tax from the local peasants, but instead of depositing the funds into a bank, the money was used for immediate local expenses, though Zenon remained officially accountable to the Treasury. Zenon likely managed these payments as the head of the local community.

*Line 6.* <term>hierá</term>: I take these to be sheep belonging to the temples <note>original: "hierà próbata"</note>. Compare other papyri which mention "holy sheep" belonging to village farmers, which editors suggest were animals intended for sacrifice. Another document contains a list of temple sheep and the names of the peasants who leased them. Interestingly, in this case, the temple sheep did not pay the tax like the other categories, or Zenon did not handle those specific funds.

*Line 13.* <term>laïká</term>: These are Crown sheep leased to the peasants <note>original: "laïkà próbata"</note>. It is unclear why the Crown sheep were taxed so much higher (two drachmae) than the privately owned sheep; perhaps this figure includes additional service charges.

*Line 15.* The Greek text <note>original: "Sosirátou Kléonos"</note> could mean "Sosiratos son of Kleon" or "Sosiratos and Kleon."

### 59396. Letter from Aristeas and Pausanias to Demeas. — 0.305 m. x 0.095 m.

Aristeas, writing in the first person despite naming Pausanias as a co-author, was likely a <term>cleruch: a Greek soldier-settler who received a land grant (kleros) from the crown</term>. In another letter, he offers to sell this land grant at a discount. Demeas was a prominent associate of Zenon in the town of Philadelphia. This letter explains that Aristeas and Pausanias could not travel with the slave delivering these letters but hope to visit Demeas in early <term>Mesore: the twelfth month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly August</term>. They have requested Demeas provide 50 <term>artabs: a unit of dry measure, roughly 30-40 liters</term> of wheat to a man named Theokles.

->Aristeas and Pausanias to Demeas, greetings. For the present it was not<-
->possible to travel with the slave who is carrying the letters, because I<-
-><gloss>at/for</gloss><-
->am troubled and Pausanias is [[in]] occupied with necessary business, but [in] the month of<-
->Mesore<-

### 59398. Account from Artemidoros. — 0 m. 34 x 0 m. 20 (pl. XVI).

This Artemidoros was the steward of Apollonios’ household, <term>ho epi tes oikias: the one in charge of the house</term> (cf. no. 59150, 16), and the account probably dates from year 28 or 29 <note>of the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus</note>, before Zenon had gone to Philadelphia. He had received 108 drachmae from the sale of wool and had spent 110 1/2 on supplies of reeds (lines 5-6, cf. no. 59085), on cleaning of the houseboys’ clothes (lines 7-9, cf. no. 59176, 251-7), on <term>plymata: washings/baths</term> for their meals and on small gifts of money to them for the festival of Arsinoe.

*Line 1.* Perhaps [account].

*Line 7. <term>Gnapitra</term>* means the fuller’s fee <note>The fuller was the ancient equivalent of a dry cleaner, cleaning and thickening raw wool or garments.</note>.
*Line 12.* Read Arsinoeia. A festival of this name was celebrated in the <term>chora: the Egyptian countryside</term> in the month of Mesore (see *P. Edg.*, no. 18, introduction), and the Arsinoe mentioned here may be the same festival, though the date does not accord with the months mentioned in the preceding lines. Or there may have been another festival kept in Alexandria on a fixed date in the Macedonian calendar.

### 59404. Letter from Asklepiades to Zenon. — 0.16 m x 0.15 m.

Written across the fibers and folded horizontally. Asklepiades, perhaps the farmer mentioned in other papyri, writes that an agent has come from Ktesikles the local steward, demanding the <term>phylakitikon: a tax paid for the maintenance of the village police or guards</term> for 110 sheep and threatening to seize them if he is not paid. They are also bidding him make an agreement about his corn at whatever price Zenon may value it. The man who is obstructing him is Alexinikos the head policeman of Syron Kome <note>Syron Kome literally translates to "Village of the Syrians."</note>.
The writer's uneducated style makes it difficult to follow his meaning.

### 59409. Letter to Zenon from Botryis. — 0.195 m × 0.115 m.

### 59412. Letter from Glaukias to Zenon. — 0.34 m x 0.09 m.

Glaukias writes that he has not yet been able to settle up about the sesame and castor-oil plants <note>original: "κρότωνος", often used for oil</note>, owing to the absence of Apollonios the manager of the oil factory, but now that the latter has returned, he hopes to arrange the matter immediately. With regard to the stolen property (?) he has received a letter from Phanias authorizing him to recover it; but as Chairon would not give it up until the arrival of Ammonios, he has not yet delivered the letter; as Ammonios however has now arrived, he is trying to recover it through him. He (Chairon?) likewise promised to give back the Chian wine. With regard to the calves, Zenon knows what has taken place. The meaning of the last two lines is rather obscure.

### **59416. Letter from Demeas to Zenon.** — 0.10 m x 0.25 m (plate XVIII).

## 59421. Petition to Zenon from Dionysios. — 0 m. 17 x 0 m. 14 and 0 m. 17 x 0 m. 14 (pl. XIX).

> Dionysios the <term>corn-measurer</term> <note>original: *sitometres*, a minor official responsible for measuring grain for taxes or distribution</note>, who seems to have been arrested on an accusation of dishonest practice, appeals to Zenon to examine the case himself or, if not, to order Artemidoros to accept sureties for his appearance until Apollonios <note>the Finance Minister of Egypt</note> arrives and holds an inquiry. He protests that he is not responsible, being merely an employee working under Nikon and Addaios, and he suggests that Zenon should give instructions to credit him with the quantities measured out on the <term>dochikon</term> standard <note>a "receiver's standard" of measurement, often larger than the standard used for distributions</note>, while for the rest he will pay up an additional ten per cent according to Apollonios’ order. He casts himself on Zenon’s mercy, regarding him as Apollonios’ equal and professing himself ready to accept his judgment.
> The mention of Artemidoros, Nikon and Addaios indicates that Dionysios was employed on the Memphite estate and that the petition dates from the early years of the correspondence.

**59426. Letter from Dromon to Zenon.** — 0 m. 14 × 0 m. 265.

Dromon reports that according to Zenon’s instructions he is taking good care that his employees are not molested. Before Zenon sails up the river in good health, let him order one of his people to buy a <term>kotyle</term> <note>a Greek unit of volume, approximately 270 milliliters or nearly half a pint</note> of Attic honey; for Dromon has been commanded by the god to buy this as a medicament for his eyes.

The letter was evidently written at a time when Zenon was staying in Alexandria. It seems probable that Dromon himself was living at Memphis and that the temple to which he resorted was the great Sarapieion at Saqqarah, where medical advice was communicated to sufferers through dreams. In any case the god must have been either Sarapis or Asklepios. Honey was by no means scarce in Egypt and is often mentioned in Egyptian recipes for ailments of the eyes; and it is a curious indication of Greek influence that even in the interior of Egypt Attic honey <note>honey from the region of Athens, highly prized for its quality in antiquity</note> should have been specially recommended.

Dromon to Zenon, greetings. We give thanks to all the gods,
if you yourself are well and other matters have gone for you according to plan.
I myself am also in good health, and just as you wrote to me, I am taking every
care so that no one may molest your people.
5 But when you sail up in good health, order one of your people
to buy a <term>kotyle</term> of Attic honey; for I have need of it for
my eyes according to the command of the God.
Farewell.

VERSO:
To Zenon.

*Line 3*. <term>we are in good health . . . myself</term> <note>original: "errōmetha . . . autos"</note> : *as written*. A reference to the exaction of taxes, as in no. 59130, 19.
*Line 4*. <term>may molest</term> <note>original: "enochlēis"</note> : perhaps with reference to the exaction of taxes, as in no. 59130, 19.
*Line 5*. <term>you sail up</term> <note>original: "anapleēis"</note> : ‘when you are about to sail up’ <note>meaning traveling south, up the Nile from Alexandria</note>. For <term>in good health</term> <note>original: "hygiainōn"</note> *compare* P. S. I., 500, 9.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Entry Journal of the Museum*, no. 48955; *P. Edg.*, 89; *WILCKEN*, *Archiv*, VIII, p. 66; *Collection*, 6804.

**59427. Letter from Epichares to Apollonios.** — 0 m. 12 × 0 m. 23 and 0 m. 115 × 0 m. 07.

As the letter is addressed to Apollonios, it probably dates from year 28 or 29. Epichares had come to see him and give a full account of his business, but finding him busy had gone away without fulfilling the object of his visit. He now sends Dionysios with a request for a supply of corn and a thousand <term>drachmæ</term> <note>silver coins used in the Hellenistic world</note> and he asks Apollonios to write and say to whom he is to repay the loan.

The letter is in two pieces, and it is not clear how much is missing between them. The restorations which I have suggested are of the right length in proportion to each other, but they may all be too long or too short.

### 59430. Account from Hermon. — 0 m. 335 X 0 m. 12.

Hermon (see no. 59244) presents an account of what he had spent on the shearing of the Arabian and Milesian sheep belonging to the estate and on the packing of the wool, besides some other small expenses. The text is interesting, as it shows that the Milesian sheep, whose fleece was protected by a covering of hide <note>original: "hypo-diphthera"</note>, were not shorn in the usual way like the Arabian sheep, but had their wool plucked out by hand. Compare Varro, *On Agriculture*, II, 11 and Pliny, *Natural History*, VIII, 37 : <note>original Latin: "oves non ubique tondentur; durat quibusdam in locis vellendi mos"</note> "sheep are not shorn everywhere; in some places the custom of plucking persists." Moreover while the Arabian fleeces were packed in matting, the more valuable Milesian wool was transported in boxes. For Apollonios’ flock of Milesian sheep see nos. 59142 and 59195.

It also introduces an account of sheep shearing and wool plucking techniques on the estate.</summary>

## 59433. Letter from Eudemos to Zenon. — 0 m. 255 x 0 m. 09 (plate XX).

Eudemos writes that he cannot leave his work, being busy with the harvest and with the wild oxen, but he has sent Theodora with the grey <term>chiton</term> <note>A basic tunic garment.</note> which Zenon had ordered. He asks Zenon to write to Philon requesting him to reduce the rent, as fifteen <term>arourai</term> <note>A unit of land measurement, roughly 2/3 of an acre.</note> of the crop are worm-eaten. He asks him also to exact the rent of the sheep from the Arabs, who are keeping possession of the wool as well as of the sheep; and he adds that he will make Ptolemaios answer before Zenon for certain sheep which he has failed to return.

### 59439. Memorandum to Zenon from Herakleides. — 0 m. 07 X 0 m. 19.

This is the Herakleides about whom we find the swineherds complaining in nos. 59330 and 59331, and who now asserts that he is being pestered by them. He had given Zenon a report about the pigs of Thoteus and now asks him to send someone to help him to bring them down before Thoteus sells them. Presumably Thoteus had leased a herd of pigs and had not yet handed over those which he owed to Zenon as rent (cf. no. 59331, lines 10-14).

->Memorandum to Zenon from Herakleides. Concerning the<-
->report which I gave to you about the pigs<-
->of Thoteus; you would do well then to send<-
->someone with me, so that I may bring them down for him before he<-
<margin>5</margin> ->sells them. For I am being hounded by the<-
->swineherds here.<-

VERSO:

->To Zenon.<-

*Lines 1-3.* In cases like this it is sometimes doubtful whether "concerning" <note>original: "περὶ"</note> goes with "memorandum" or forms the beginning of the main sentence.
*Line 2. Thoteus:* see no. 59330, line 3.
*Line 4. for him:* <note>original: "αὐτῶ"</note> for "to him" (referring to the messenger) or perhaps a slip of the pen for "them" (the pigs).

### 59440. Memorandum from Herakleotes. — 0 m. 21 X 0 m. 16.

Herakleotes was a young musician who was being trained to take part in public competitions. Demeas, the late head of the gymnasium <note>original: "palæstra"; a wrestling school or sports ground where intellectual and musical education also took place.</note> in Philadelphia, had left him in his will a musical instrument and had assigned him an allowance to enable him to complete his training. We know this from an interesting papyrus in the British Museum. The present text is a request from Herakleotes, probably addressed to one of his guardians, Zenon or Nestos, for an advance of two months’ salary and food allowance. See also *P.S.I.*, 1011.

->[. . .] the expense for the month comes to:<-
->for oil, 1 drachma, 6 obols, 1/4 obol — for the bath, 6 [obols?] 1/4 obol<-
->for fish, 2 drachmae, 1/4 obol; so that for the month it is 4 drachmae, 6 obols, 1/4 obol<-

*Line 2.* <note>The symbol ⦂ is used here to denote a quarter of an obol in place of the usual abbreviation for "tetarton".</note>

*Line 17.* Possibly "monthly," but the following letters are unclear.
*Line 18. of the:* or perhaps "of each [month]?"

# 59443. Petition to Zenon from Thamoys. — 0 m. 175 X 0 m. 105.

Written along the fibers and folded horizontally. Thamoys the swineherd complains that, while doing something to protect the pigs against the crocodiles, he had been assaulted by Psosnaus. He is still bedridden and has been obliged to hire a man to keep the pigs at their task of treading the corn, and he has sent the present letter by his wife. Zenon is requested to summon the aggressor and question the witnesses, so that justice may be done.
The petition is written in a good hand, but in unconnected sentences full of grammatical mistakes.

[To Zenon greetings] Thamoys the swineherd [ ... ]
[ ... ]. I am being wronged by
[Psosnaus ... ] at the river
[ ... lest] a crocodile tear apart
5 [the pig? ... ], Psosnaus, intercepting me
[laid hands] on me and [ ... ] the [wife? ...]

*Line 1. swineherd:* probably for <note>original: "ὑοφορβός"</note>.
*Line 3. Read* Psosnautos or Psosnaus. — [ ... ]ntos: *probably the genitive of a participle agreeing with* "me", *whether expressed or understood.*
*Line 5. Perhaps* pig <note>original: "δέλφακα"</note> or sacrificial animals <note>original: "ἱερεῖα"</note>. — intercepting: <note>original: "παραλαβών"</note>.
*Line 6. "hands"* <note>original: "χέρας"</note> is rather long for the gap; perhaps "violence" <note>original: "βίαν"</note>.

Translation: "When he has trodden the seed in with his pigs, he waits for the harvest; then, having used the pigs to thresh the grain, he gathers it in."</note>
*Line 12*. "Carrying" <note>original: "Φέρων"</note>: should be read as the feminine form <note>original: "Φέρουσαν"</note> since it refers to the wife.
*Line 16*. "So that" <note>original: "ἵνα"</note>: a round blot between the letters 'n' and 'a' might be read as 'th', but is probably accidental.

## 59445. Memorandum to Zenon from Theophilos. — 0 m. 215 x 0 m. 165 (pl. XXI).

> Theophilos was a painter, who apparently came from Alexandria (as seen in *P.S.I.*, 407, 14) and was employed by Zenon to paint the house of Diotimos (see no. 59193). In

<column-break/>

<page-num>171</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>
<sig>22.</sig>

this memorandum he gives an estimate of the cost of painting certain parts of four rooms. The estimate is based on the assumption that he will provide his own materials. If these are provided for him, the cost will be reduced from 53 to 30 drachmae. The text is peculiarly interesting, as our knowledge of ancient house-painting has till now been derived almost entirely from archaeological and not from literary evidence. See a short but comprehensive article by Rostovtzeff in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*, XXXIX, pp. 144-163.

->Memorandum [to Zeno]n from Theophi-<-
->l[os] the con[tract]or regarding the works<-
->[in] the house of Diotimos. In the porch<-
->[...] so that a purple wavy-molding may be painted<-
-><gloss>5</gloss> and a multi-colored frieze <note>original: "θρᾶνος"</note> and a<-
->vetch-colored parapet and the lower course<-
->with a veined-border, if I provide everything<-
->myself, 30 drachmae; and for the seven-couch room<-
->to make the vaulted ceiling like the<-
-><gloss>10</gloss> pattern you saw, and to color the parapet<-
->with a desirable finish and to paint the Lesbian molding,<-
->if I provide everything myself, 20 drachmae;<-
->and [for] the five-couch rooms I will paint the<-
->wavy-moldings, if I provide everything myself, 3 drachmae.<-

*Line 2*. "Contractor" <note>original: "ἐργολάβου"</note> seems the most probable reading. "Painter" <note>original: "ζωγράφου"</note>, by which name Theophilos calls himself in other documents, is not possible, nor is "encaustic painter" <note>original: "ἐγκαυτοῦ"</note>; moreover, encaustic painting (using hot wax) was only used on the woodwork of houses, not on the walls.
*Line 5*. A frieze <note>original: "θρᾶνος"</note> was the upper part of the wall below the molding or cornice. Hesychius defines frieze-painters as "decorous wall-painters." The adjective "multi-colored" <note>original: "ποικίλος"</note> recalls the name of the famous Painted Stoa in Athens.
*Lines 5-6*. A parapet <note>original: "θωρακῖον"</note> is a natural expression for the breast-high division of the wall, especially if it was painted in imitation of architecture.
*Line 6*. Lower course <note>original: "ὑποστύλιον"</note>: probably the lowest part of the wall, below the parapet. The name suggests an architectural design.
*Line 7*. Veined-border <note>original: "φλεβοπεριμέτριον"</note>: the reader can judge from the plate whether the word can be deciphered otherwise. If rightly read, it may denote an imitation of the veining of alabaster; common in Alexandrian decor.
*Line 9*. Vaulted ceiling <note>original: "καμάραν"</note>.
*Line 10*. A round spot above the line is probably a blot.
*Line 11*. "Lesbian molding" <note>original: "τὸ Λέσβιον"</note>: specifically referring to a wavy molding.

<summary>This page contains the conclusion of a petition regarding an assault and the start of a detailed painting contract. The painting estimate is historically significant as it provides rare literary evidence for the specific terminology and costs of interior decoration in Ptolemaic Egypt.</summary>

### 59447. Letter to Zenon from Theon. — 0 m. 17 X 0 m. 115 and 0 m. 15 X 0 m. 05.

The right half of the papyrus is in Florence and has been already published in *P. S. I.*, 680. The text is written along the fibers and the letter was folded horizontally.

<column-break/>

<page-num>173</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

Theon, who had been recommended to Zenon by the lately departed Epharmostos(?), acknowledges that he is being treated with generosity, but begs for some regular work in order that he may feel justified in accepting Zenon’s bounty and that Zenon may have the satisfaction of receiving something in return. He scorns the idea of wishing to be idle and asks Zenon to assign him a lodging and all things necessary, so that he may be free from anxiety in his old age.
If <term>Epharmostos</term> <note>a person's name</note> is rightly restored in line 1, the letter must be one of the latest in our collection, for Epharmostos was still alive in year 2 (no. 59346), probably also in year 5 (no. 59362).

To Zenon, greetings. I am Theon, the one recommended to you by the late <note>original: "μακαρίτου"; literally "blessed," a term used for the deceased</note> Epharmostos. For other things I am grateful, as I receive every care from you, but I ask you—if I seem to you to be speaking [the truth]—to appoint me to some task, so that I may provide service to you by performing <margin>5</margin> my duties blamelessly, in order that I may receive what is given by you more justly, and you may give it more gladly because I am providing something more to you. If for the present time we have decided to keep quiet, you yourself will know. But you would do well to give instructions so that I may be shown a place where I might have a house and other necessities, so that <margin>10</margin> in my old age I do not wander about. For it is not proper for me to flee to any other person, since I was recommended to you from the beginning.

*Line 3. The letter before the gap seems to be 'a' or 'l';* the truth <note>original: "ἀληθῆ"</note> *or* pleasing things <note>original: "ἀρεστά"</note> *would be of the right length.*

B<small>IBL.</small>: *Journal d'entrée du Musée, no. 48975.*

### 59451. Letter to Zenon from two Sacred Servants of Boubastis. — 0 m. 265 x 0 m. 13.

Two feeders of cats, attached to the cult of Boubastis <note>the Egyptian goddess Bastet, often depicted as a cat</note> in the village of Sophthis, state that the king and likewise Apollonios had ordered that persons of their profession should be exempt from compulsory labor throughout the country. But Leontiskos the chief policeman (see no. 59145) had sent them to work at the harvest (which they did, not wishing to trouble Zenon) and has now sent them off to make bricks, leaving in peace for his own ends two professional brick-makers in the same village. They therefore appeal to Zenon to conform to the order of the king and the <term>dioiketes</term> <note>the chief financial minister of Ptolemaic Egypt</note>.

->To Zenon, greetings, the sacred servants of Bou-<-
->bastis who are cat-feeders. Doing<-
->well, the king has exempted this class<-
->throughout the country from compulsory<-
5 ->labor, and likewise also Apollonios.<-

->ontiskos therefore having forced us, sent<-
->us to the harvest, and in order<-
->that we might not trouble you, we performed<-

->and Apollonios the manager<-
20 ->instructed, and you having followed<-
->likewise; for against whom...<-

Line 5. The prominence given to Apollonios (see the remarks of <term>Wilcken</term>, *in the place cited*) is due not merely to his official position, but also to the fact that he was the great landlord in this district and Zenon's employer. Apollonios' care for religious cults, both Greek and Egyptian, comes out clearly in many of the Zenon papyri, in one of which we find him granting a small allotment to a <term>sacred feeder</term> <note>original: "ἱεροβοσκός"</note>.
Line 6. The papyrus has *ex-Sophthis*, which may be resolved either into *ek* or into *ex Sophthis* (<term>Mayser</term>, *Grammar*, I, p. 225). For the position of this village see no. 59145.

### 59454. Letter from Hippokrates to Nikanor. — 0 m. 175 x 0 m. 285.

In this letter, remarkable for its frank expression of resentment, Hippokrates accuses Nikanor of continually trying to injure him. Putting aside the question whether the 1000 drachmae should be exacted from himself or his surety <note>a "surety" is a person who takes responsibility for another's debt</note>, Nikanor had no right to enter the house of a free-born woman, where Hippokrates happened to be living, and to put a seal on her possessions as if they were seizable for the debt. The lady will take steps to secure justice as soon as Hermaphilos the steward <note>original: "oikonomos"; a high-ranking financial official</note> returns. As for himself, let Nikanor insult him and haul him to prison, leaving his surety unmolested; he will try to defend himself; and he tells his oppressor plainly what he and all other people in the town think about his "amiable" character.

Hippokrates is probably the joint farmer of the <term>apomoira</term> <note>a tax of one-sixth on the produce of vineyards and orchards, dedicated to the cult of Arsinoe Philadelphos</note> mentioned in number 59367, and the 1000 drachmae may represent a shortage in his payments to the Treasury. Nikanor seems to have been an official subordinate to the chief steward, acting in the present case as a <term>praktor</term> <note>a debt collector or bailiff responsible for enforcing payments</note>; among the persons of that name who appear in the papyri I would identify him with the Nikanor of *P.S.I.*, 659, 12. The mention of Hermaphilos shows that the letter dates from the early years of Ptolemy Euergetes, and we know that at that time Zenon was closely associated with the farmers of the tax.

The note on the reverse is in a different hand and deals with a different subject.

Hippokrates to Nikanor, greetings. It is not now for the first time that you are [attemp]ting to do me wrong, but you always continue to treat me with drunken insolence, looking down on my simple-mindedness. If [you indeed think], against the facts, that the collection of the 1,000 drachmae must be from me and not from [the surety], surely it was not yet necessary for you [to enter] another’s house, where I ha[ppen to be], 5 to treat a free-born woman with drunken insolence and to place seals upon another’s [furniture, to which] you have no right at all. But concerning these matters, Autexila, the lady of [the house], [if she wi]shes, will help herself as soon as Hermaphilos arrives and [provides the opportunity] to obtain justice from you. As for me—so that you do not [disturb] the surety—10 as for me, if you are able, both insult me and haul me away. For I shall try [to help] myself. However, realize that you are an offensive person, and the more one takes care of you [ ... ], the more you trample upon them. And I am not the only one saying this, b[ut all] those in the city; you are so "dear to everyone" <note>original: "pasiphilos"; Hippokrates is using the term sarcastically to mean "notoriously disliked"</note>.
->Fare[well]. Year [ ... ]<-

*Line 1. [attempting]: this and the following reconstructions are merely suggestions, to show briefly what I take to be the meaning of the text.*
*Line 2. "despising me for my simplicity" <note>original: "καταγνούς μου τῆς εὐηθίας"</note>; but of course the sentence might be otherwise restored.*
*Lines 4-6. Perhaps the plea of Nikanor was that he regarded the woman as Hippokrates' wife.*
*Line 12. city: probably Krokodilopolis or Philadelphia, not Alexandria.*

### 59457. Memorandum to Zenon from Kleon. — 0 m. 105 $\times$ 0 m. 11 (pl. XVII).

Written along the fibers and folded horizontally. The text is a reminder about the allowances due to the writer and his mother for personal expenses in the month of Epeiph <note>The eleventh month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly June/July</note>. Kleon addresses Zenon as "father," but the gist of the memorandum and the way in which the mother is mentioned make it somewhat doubtful whether Zenon actually was his father. The allowance, both in amount and in detail, is so similar to that of Herakleotes (no. 59440) that I am more inclined to regard Kleon as a lad under Zenon's protection being trained in a gymnasium, like Pyrrhos (no. 59060) and the above-mentioned Herakleotes, either for musical or for athletic contests. *P.S.I.*, 528 is a similar petition from Kleon on the same subject, and in this he speaks about the festival of Hermes and the festival of the Muses <note>original: "τὰ Ἑρμαῖα καὶ τὰ Μουσεῖα"</note> and again mentions his mother. I fancy that the lady was not much more than a servant-girl <note>original: "παιδίσκη"</note>, whether Kleon was Zenon's son or merely one of the promising boys whom he picked out and educated as a likely winner in the games (cf. *P.S.I.*, 340, 24).

Memorandum to Zenon
the father, from Kleon.
Regarding what I am to receive
as wages for Epeiph:
<margin>5</margin> for oil and meat, 5 drachmae;
for relish <note>original: "ὄψον"; cooked food eaten with bread</note>, 2 drachmae; for castor oil <note>original: "χίκιος"</note>, ...
for washing, ... for spices...

*Line 7. For washing: <note>original: "πλυσίμων"</note>; "for the laundry."*

### 59460. Petition to the king from Korragos. — 0.255 m x 0.135 m (pl. XX).

The writer had bought certain house property in Theadelphia and Pharbaithos, formerly belonging to Telestes and lately sold by the <term>praktor</term> <note>a government official responsible for collecting debts or seizing property</note>. Some time after, though he had paid the price and entered into possession, the agents of the <term>praktor</term>

---

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

declared that some parts of the property did not belong to him and were now attempting to sell these. He therefore asks the king to order the <term>dioiketes</term> <note>the chief financial minister of Egypt</note> or the strategos <note>the provincial governor</note> to examine the case and do justice to whichever party succeeds in proving its claim.

Korragos is the author of no. 59232, in which he again mentions his son Attalos. Of Telestes, often mentioned in the Zenon and Hibeh papyri, we know little except that he was a man of high standing with possessions in the Fayoum and perhaps elsewhere. From an unpublished papyrus in the British Museum, <term>ROSTOVTZEFF</term> <note>Mikhail Rostovtzeff, a prominent 20th-century historian of the ancient world</note> in *Large Estate*, p. 176, has drawn the conclusion that his possessions were confiscated and sold up in the 6th year of Euergetes; and the present text confirms this inference in a very satisfactory manner.

The form of the petition varies remarkably from the ordinary types studied by Collomp in his *Research on the Chancery and Diplomacy of the Ptolemies* <note>original: "Recherches sur la chancellerie et la diplomatique des Lagides"</note>. How it came into Zenon’s possession I cannot say.

->To [King Pto]lemy, greetings, Korra-<-
->[gos. In the A]rsinoite nome <note>The Fayoum region</note>, in Thea-<-
->[delphia and] Pharbaithos, the lodgings<-
->[of Telestes] and all the appurten-<-
<margin>5</margin>->[ances...] being sold<-
->[by the pra]ktor, I purchased for<-
->[my sons A]ndromenes and Attalos<-
->[... which Te]lestes possessed. After I<-
->[gave the] price and was in possession<-
<margin>10</margin>->[... ] just as I have written to you,<-
->[after fifte]en months, the assis-<-
->[tants of the prak]tor [took] some parts of<-
->[ ]...<-
->[ ] and are attempting to<-
<margin>15</margin>->[sell them. If] then it seems good to you, you would<-
->[do well] by ordering the dioiketes<-

*Line 5.* For example, "fittings" or "outbuildings" <note>original: "χρηστήρια"</note>.

*Line 7.* sons: in no. 59232 Korragos writes "my son Attalos," but the petition is in a different hand and probably his spelling varied with his scribe.

*Line 8.* Some such phrase as "whatever he once" <note>original: "ὅσα ποτέ"</note> is required in the gap.

*Lines 15-16.* you would [do well] <note>original: "καλῶς ἂν [ποιήσαις]"</note>: <term>COLLOMP</term>, in the work cited above, p. 135, remarks of this formula that "addressed to the king it would have been, no doubt, an impropriety: we see that one can allow oneself to address it to an official." It would be safer to say that in formal petitions addressed to the king the phrase is scarcely ever found.

*Line 16.* "Ordering" <note>original: "συντάξας"</note> seems to me certain, though the usual word in such cases is "commanding" <note>original: "προστάξας"</note>.

### 59462. Letter from Kriton to Zenon. — 0.145 m x 0.345 m.

The author of this amusing piece complains about a certain person who had been billeted on him <term>Billeted: a system where soldiers or officials were legally entitled to stay in private homes</term> in order to carry out some work. Up till now he had done nothing. But, while Kriton was sleeping in the fields, he proceeded to drive the sow out of the courtyard, rousing up Kriton's wife by threatening to hamstring the beast and calling provocatively on Kriton himself, whom he supposed to be indoors. The wife told all this to Kriton on his return, but he had reported it to no one, waiting until the time required for the work should have passed; and meanwhile he kept the sow out of the courtyard. He now appeals to Zenon in the name of the Brother Gods <note>Ptolemy II and Arsinoe II</note> and the king to finish his affair and not allow him to be insulted any longer, swearing by the spirit <term>Daimon: the divine "genius" or guardian spirit of the king</term> of the king and by Berenike that he had not received from the fellow so much as one brick.

<column-break/>

<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>
<page-num>183</page-num>

The oaths date the letter to the reign of Euergetes <note>Ptolemy III Euergetes, 246–222 BC</note>, and this Kriton is not to be confused with the commander of the fleet mentioned in the early correspondence.

Kriton to Zenon, greetings. You would do well to take an interest on my behalf,
so that I am not 
ruined for a longer time. For although [he promised] me to settle matters by the twentieth,
he has done nothing,
but even while I was sleeping in the field, he threw the sow out of the courtyard at night,
even though she was pregnant,
and he called out to my wife, saying he would hamstring the animal, and he challenged me,
supposing
<margin>5</margin> me to be sleeping inside. When I arrived from the field, my wife reported to me
everything that happened.
But I revealed nothing of this to anyone until the days he requested
should pass;
and I did not bring the sow into the courtyard anymore. I entreat you, then, by the 
Brothers and the king
to settle my affairs, so that these things no longer happen and I am no longer
insulted for any more time.
And I swear to you by the King’s spirit and Queen Berenike—so that you do not think
I am adjuring him 
<margin>10</margin> merely to insult him—that I have not received even one single brick from him. You, therefore,
take great care 
concerning these things.
->Farewell.<-

REVERSE SIDE:

->To Zenon.<-

<note>
Line 2. Kriton does not give the name of the other person; the text ends in a word like "having promised" <note>original: "ταξάμενος"</note>. For the date, "on the twentieth" <note>original: "εἰκάδι"</note> is written where "by the twentieth" <note>original: "εἰκάδα"</note> is meant.
Line 4. The word for "saying" <note>original: "φάμενος"</note> is doubtful.
Line 7. Note the mention of "the Brothers" <note>original: "τῶν ἀδελφῶν"</note> without the word "Gods," contrary to what the scholar Wilcken says.
Line 9. "The King's spirit" <note>original: "τὸν βασιλέως δαίμονα"</note>: the use of "King" without the article "the" is a traditional formula.
Line 10. "One brick": possibly a proverbial expression for "nothing at all," but likely literal here, referring to a contract for building materials.
</note>

## 59466. Letter to Zenon from Meieus. — 0 m. 24 x 0 m. 11.

The writer had a legal dispute against Stachys, and Zenon had instructed him to have the case tried in Stachys's home town, likely Krokodilopolis <note>A major city in the Arsinoite Nome (Fayum), modern-day Faiyum</note>. Meieus objects to this, fearing a "home court advantage," and demands that the trial take place in a city where both parties are outsiders, such as Memphis or Herakleopolis. He adds that Pasis, upon hearing that his own case was to be heard in Krokodilopolis, fled in despair to the "altar of the king" <note>Seeking sanctuary or asylum at a royal altar was a common way to escape perceived injustice or arrest in Ptolemaic Egypt</note>. The letter is written across the grain of the papyrus and was folded horizontally. A man named Meieus, an "Isionomos" <note>An official or priest of the goddess Isis</note>, is mentioned in document no. 59172, and another Meieus, a bee-keeper, appears in no. 59520; it is uncertain if either is our writer.

> Meieus to Zenon, greetings.
> [ . . . ] me because we are not [being judged <note>original: "κρινόμεθα"</note>]
> [against] Stachys; you requested me to be judged in
> [that man's] city. Indeed, you did [not] decide
> <margin>5</margin> [justly]; for we shall be set aside [ . . . ]
> [ . . . ]; but let him also be judged
> [as a] stranger, just as we are, whether he [wishes]
> in Memphis, or in Herakleopolis;
> [for] thus it is just. You would [therefore]
> <margin>10</margin> do well to give orders accordingly.
> [And] Pasis, hearing that it is necessary to be [judged]
> against him in Krokodilopolis, [withdrew]
> to the altar of the [king].
> <margin>15</margin> ->Farewell.<-

<note>Line 2. The missing word may have been a participle, or, as is more probable, "you requested" <note>original: "ἠξίωσας"</note> may have begun a new sentence.</note>
<note>Lines 4-5. "decide justly" <note>original: "δικαίως ἔθου"</note> is suggested by the length of the gap and the remains of letters, but the phrase seems rather a doubtful one.</note>
<note>Line 5. "we shall be set aside" <note>original: "ἀποθησόμεθα"</note>: the meaning is not clear; one would have expected a passive verb, such as "we shall be left behind." — "under her/it" <note>original: "ὑφ’ αὑτήν"</note>: probably meaning under the city's jurisdiction, followed by "having been led" or "having been judged." But "by themselves" <note>original: "ὑφ’ αὑτῶν"</note> might equally well be read.</note>
<note>Line 13. The altar of the king is mentioned again in a demotic oath from Zenon's archives.</note>

**Bibliography** : *Museum Entry Register, no. 48996.*

<header>ZENON PAPYRI. 187</header>

## 59467. Petition to Zenon from the bee-keepers of the Arsinoite province. — 0 m. 17 x 0 m. 22.

Zenon had ordered the bee-keepers to send their donkeys to the village of Philadelphia to work for ten days. They complain that he has kept the animals for eighteen days, leaving them with no way to transport their hives back from the summer pastures. The local farmers are now warning them that the fields are about to be flooded (irrigation) and the brushwood burned to clear the land. Unless the donkeys return immediately, the hives will be destroyed, and the king’s tax revenue will suffer. They promise to return with the donkeys once the hives are safe. The ancient practice of moving bees to different feeding grounds in portable hives still exists in Egypt today.

> To Zenon, greetings from the bee-keepers of the Arsinoite
> province. You wrote concerning the beasts of burden <term>hypozygion: pack animals, specifically donkeys in this context</term> so that they might arrive
> at Philadelphia and work for 10 <term>Greek numeral: ι</term> days. But it is
> already 18 <term>Greek numeral: ιη</term> days since they have been working, and the [beehives]
> <margin>5</margin> have been left in the field and it is the time for bringing
> them back and we have no beasts of burden to carry them up. We pay
> no small tax <term>phoros: a fixed rental or tax paid in kind (honey/wax) or money</term> to the king. If you do not send
> the beasts of burden as quickly as possible, it will result in the hives being lost
> and the tax failing. And now the farmers warn us,
> <margin>10</margin> saying: ‘We are releasing the water and we are burning the brushwood. If you
> do not remove them, you will lose them.’ We therefore beg you, if it seems good to you,
> to send our beasts of burden, so that we may remove them. And when
> we have removed them and you have need of them, we will be present again.
> ->Farewell.<-

<note>Line 2. "beasts of burden" <note>original: "ὑποζυγίων"</note>: unless "our" in line 12 is a mistake for "to us," the donkeys belonged to the bee-keepers and had been borrowed by Zenon for work on his estate.</note>
<note>Line 5. "have been left" <note>original: "ἔρρηται"</note>: This means "deposited" or left out in the open.</note>
<note>Line 7. "tax" <note>original: "φόρον"</note>: The nature of this tax is not entirely clear, but other documents show that hives were largely private property. It is doubtful whether there was a special class of "royal bee-keepers"; more likely the same tax was collected from everyone.</note>
<note>Line 10. "releasing" <note>original: "ἀφίoμεν"</note>: written this way in the original text.</note>
<note>Line 12. "to send" <note>original: "ἀποστεῖλαι"</note>: the letter 'p' was corrected over a 'ph' in the manuscript.</note>

**Bibliography** : *Museum Entry Register, no. 48997*; *Papyri Edgar*, 106; Wilcken, *Archive*, VIII, p. 68; *Sammelbuch*, 6989.

24.

### 59470. Letter from Molossos to Zenon. — 0.14 m. x 0.26 m.

Molossos was an agent employed by Zenon and his superior, the finance minister Apollonios, as a commercial traveler. Here, he reports that another agent named Theogenes arrived in the city of Mendes with samples of flax. Local merchants indicated there was high demand for the product. Molossos urges Zenon to send more flax quickly and to involve the local banker, Promethion. He also mentions a previous message about papyrus rolls sent via a man named Kriton. This letter provides a vivid look at how trade was conducted in the Egyptian interior during the 3rd century BCE. The right side of the papyrus is missing; the bracketed text represents the editor's best guesses.

Mol[ossos] to Zenon, greetings. After writing you the first [letter, which]
[was delivered to you by] Horos, our associate, Theogenes arrived in Mendes on the 23rd of the month Me[cheir? <note>Roughly February</note>,]
[bringing three sealed] bundles of flax-straw which [you entrusted] to him; they are being sold at [ . . . each;]
and when the retail-dealers <term>kapeloi</term> <note>Small-scale market merchants</note> were asked if they could be sold, they told me [they could dispose of 10,000.]
5 [Therefore, as far as] it is profitable for you, send as quickly as possible both [the goods] and someone to manage the sale; [instruct him also to see to]

*Line 2. The month is likely Mecheir or Mesore.*

*Line 3. The Greek word "ana" was followed by the specific price, now lost.*

*Line 5. It is unclear if "the one who will manage the sale" refers to a new person being sent or someone already present.*

### 59472. Letter to Zenon from Nektosiris. — 0.165 m. x 0.16 m.

Nektosiris, a manufacturer of tow <term>stippuon</term> <note>Coarse fiber from flax or hemp used to make rope and heavy cloth.</note>, asks Zenon to write to Hermolaos and Petosiris, the royal scribe in Aphroditopolis, to have his partners brought back, as they owe him wages for work; for as soon as Zenon went away, they abandoned him. ### 59475. Memorandum from Nikias to Zenon. — 0.195 m. x 0.11 m. (plate XXIII).

Nikias had sent a female foal to Boutos to graze on the hay. Next day she ran off to find her dam, taking the road she was accustomed to. The guards at Simyra seized and locked her up. A guard from Boutos together with a brother-in-law of Nikias followed on her tracks and had taken possession of her, when Noumenios the guard came up and led them off to prison. Zenon is therefore requested to write to Noumenios and explain the matter.
The memorandum is written in short, but lively sentences with few connecting particles. Whether the author is the Nikias of no. 59474 is quite doubtful, but there is at least no doubt that the two letters were not written by the same scribe.

->Memorandum from Nikias<-
->To Zenon. On the seventh, we sent<-
->to Boutos in the Memphite nome a female foal<-
->to graze on the hay.<-
<margin>5</margin> ->She ran away on the eighth,<-
->seeking her mother. And she went<-
->by the road she was accustomed to travel.<-
->The guards from Simyra<-
->caught her and locked her up.<-
<margin>10</margin> ->A guard from Boutos and a certain<-
->brother-in-law of mine followed<-
->her tracks. When they arrived, they took<-
->possession of the beast of burden. When<-
->Noumenios the guard arrived,<-
<margin>15</margin> ->he also led them away [to prison].<-
->I beg you then, if it seems good to you,<-
->to write to him about these matters.<-
->Farewell.<-

*Line 3.* "Foal": the runaway was probably not a horse filly, but a young she-ass (see "beast of burden" <note>original: "ὑποζυγίου"</note> in line 13 and no. 59476).
*Line 15.* "Led them away": the subject is of course Noumenios.

### 59480. Letter to Zenon from Paapis. — 0.335 m. x 0.075 m.

Paapis had made some request about a house which he had built and in accordance with Zenon’s order he now gives a statement of the expenses. The details are interesting.

| | |
|:---|:---|
| For 5,500 bricks, at 15 drachmae <note>The drachma was the standard silver or bronze coin of the era.</note> the 10,000 | 8 dr. 1 1/2 ob. <note>An obol was 1/6th of a drachma.</note> |
| For donkeys, at 15 dr. the 10,000 bricks | 8 dr. 1 1/2 ob. |
| To builders, at 7 dr. the 10,000 bricks | 3 dr. 5 ob. |
| To carriers, at 6 dr. the 10,000 bricks | 3 dr. |
| [Wood-work?] | 2 dr. |
| One window | 1 1/2 ob. |
| [ ] | 1/2 ob. |
| Reeds for the roof | 1 1/2 ob. |
| **TOTAL** | **25 dr. 5 1/2 ob.** |

It was evidently a very small house made of mud bricks; the floor was probably of stamped mud and the roof of mud-plastered reeds supported on palm-wood rafters; the window would be either a shutter or a wooden grating, and there was no doubt a wooden door. The two chief items of expense were the cost of the bricks and the cost of transporting them by donkey from the brick-field. The <term>oikodomoi</term> <note>original: "οἰκοδόμοι"</note> were the brick-layers, the <term>ergatai</term> <note>original: "ἐργάται"</note> the men or boys who carried for them.

> [the price per] myriad <note>10,000 units</note>: 15 drachmae / 8 dr. 4.5 ob.

### 59481. Letter to Zenon from Paesis. — 0.37 m. x 0.09 m.

Paesis, one of the potters engaged by Zenon to make jars for the requirements of the estate, writes to show how zealous he is for his employer’s interests. He calls attention to the likelihood that some of the potters who are coating the inside of the jars with pitch may be careless and give some of them a double coat, and to prevent any waste of pitch he proposes that he himself along with three others should be put in charge of the work. The potters, he says, bear him malice, saying that he is always writing against them to Zenon; but he pays no heed to them and is determined to report everything that Zenon ought to know. He has lately delivered to Anosis 2000 jar-lids, while the other potters have delivered nothing; wherefore they regard him with an evil eye.

->esis. In order that it may not hap-<-
->pen that the potters who are <-
->pitch-coating in some [jars]...<-

He finds that it is "a true resin, i.e. not gum-resin, and is neither pitch nor bitumen. Wine stored in a jar so treated would acquire a slight flavor of resin, such as that imparted to much modern Greek wine by the deliberate addition of resin, and it is suggested that the present practice originated from the acquired taste due to the old necessity to use resin in order to make the wine-jars impermeable".

### 59482. Memorandum to Zenon from Pathiophis. — 0.24 m. X 0.12 m.

Pathiophis, one of Zenon's farmers (see no. 59292), pleads with his employer to release his wife from prison, as she is wearing out her heart over her children and he himself is unable to attend to his work. Let him take pity on them this time; and if ever he finds them doing the like again, they will ask no mercy. The chief interest of the text is the pathetic appeal which it makes to Zenon's feelings.

### 59483. Letter to Zenon from Pais. — 0 m. 25 × 0 m. 105.

Pais asks Zenon to give him, by order, some money for caulking the boat, as he is about to sail down the river, also ten large nails, corn allowance from the 15th of Mecheir <note>A month in the Egyptian calendar, roughly February to March.</note> and the rest of his salary. He has already received from Petechonsis a jar of wine and three drachmae in the month of Pachons <note>Roughly May to June.</note>.
The author may be the Pais mentioned in *P. S. I.*, 382, who writes to Zenon about the repairing of a boat, possibly also the author of *P. Edg.*, 111.

> Pais to Zenon, greetings.
> If it seems good to you, order
> that there be given for the caulking
> of the boat whatever seems right
> 5 to you, for we are ready
> to sail downriver, so that it may
> not suffer any damage and
> we have trouble, and ten
> eight-finger <note>Approximately 6 inches or 15 cm long.</note> nails,
> 10 and the corn allowance
> from the 15th of Mecheir and
> <unclear>...for</unclear>
> <unclear>the</unclear> voyage downriver
> and the rest of my
> 14 salary. I have also received
> from Petechonsis
> a jar of wine
> and 3 drachmae in copper
> for the month of Pachons.
> 20 Good fortune.

*Line 2.* order <note>original: "συντάξαι"</note>: the employment of the infinitive for the imperative is in this and many other cases due to the influence of the preceding "it seems good" <note>original: "δοκεῖ"</note>.
*Line 8.* Compare *P. Edg.*, 111, 34, "8 nails for steering-paddles" <note>original: "ἥλοι πηδαλίων η"</note>.
*Lines 12-13.* It seems scarcely possible to read "so that we may have for" <note>original: "ἵ]να ἔ[χωμ]εν εἰς"</note>, for the first word in line 13 looks like "but" <note>original: "δέ"</note>.
*Line 18.* "in copper" <note>original: "χαλκῶν"</note>: 'of money'.
*Lines 18-19.* Written on a smudged surface; probably something has been deleted.

Bibl. : *Journal d’entrée du Musée*, no. 49012.

### 59484. Memorandum to Zenon from Pais. — 0 m. 40 × 0 m. 165.

Pais the carpet-weaver had already presented to Zenon a denunciation of his fellow-workman Nechthembes and now adds some proofs of his knavery. The carpet weighed

<column-break/>

<page-num>201</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>
<sig>26</sig>

yesterday had been damped to make it heavier, and it has turned out to be under the proper weight; he has also curtailed the length and breadth of the carpets, so that they are too small for a couch; and when they were to be weighed, he put some additional material into the scale; for all which things he deserves to have his hands cut off. Moreover he has corrupted the other weavers; and, if Zenon will allow the test, Pais with the same material will make sixteen carpets to their fourteen. When Nechthembes heard of the denunciation, he attempted to run away, but Pais arrested him and sent him to prison. And these facts he has disclosed to prevent Zenon being cheated and for his own greater credit.

Rostovtzeff <note>Michael Rostovtzeff (1870–1952), a famous historian of the ancient economy.</note>, *Large Estate*, p. 116, supposes that the factory belonged to the State and that Zenon was merely an intermediary between the State and the workmen. The weaving establishment at Memphis seems to have been created and controlled by Apollonios (nos. 59080 and 59142), and I do not see why the carpet factory likewise should not have been another of his private enterprises. But it is often difficult to distinguish between private property and State property.

> Memorandum to Zenon from Pais
> the carpet-weaver. Regarding the information I gave you about
> Nechthembes the carpet-weaver, who is
> a troublemaker, it has appeared in truth that he has embezzled
> 5 from the double-shorn carpets <note>A type of luxury rug with a thick pile on both sides.</note>. The one weighed yesterday was still
> damp and turned out to be lighter by 6 minae <note>A mina is a unit of weight, roughly 400-600 grams.</note>. And he has committed
> other acts even more absurd than these, regarding which,
> if you wish to investigate, it is just
> to cut off his hands. For he has made
> 10 the length of the carpets shorter by a cubit <note>About 18 inches or 45 cm.</note>
> and the width by two palms <note>About 6 inches or 15 cm.</note>, so that
> they do not fit a couch; and when they were about to weigh
> the carpets, he placed upon
> the scale the warp-thread as well. It is not right, therefore,
> 15 that things be this way. In addition to committing these acts,
> he has also corrupted the rest of the
> carpet-weavers. If it therefore seems good to you and you allow me...

*Line 3.* "of Nechthembes" <note>original: "Νεχθεμβέως"</note>: the ordinary and correct form is *Nechthembeous*.
*Lines 5-6.* Compare Aristophanes, *Frogs*, 1386: "Because he put in a river, making the words damp like wool-sellers do, just like the wool." <note>An ancient literary joke about dishonest merchants adding water to wool to increase its weight on the scale.</note> I do not know whether "lighter 6 minae" <note>original: "ἐλάσσω μν Ϛ"</note> means 'lighter than' or 'lighter by 6 minae', but lines 8-12 are an argument for the latter interpretation.
*Line 10.* "of a cubit" <note>original: "πήχεως"</note>: 'by a cubit'.
*Line 14.* "warp-thread" <note>original: "στήμονα"</note>: the meaning of the word in this context is not clear.
*Line 16.* "has also been corrupting" <note>original: "προσδιέφθειρεν"</note>.
*Line 17.* "you allow" <note>original: "ἐάσης"</note>: as written.

*Catalogue of the Museum, no. 59298.*

### 59488. Letter from Paramonos to Zenon. — 0 m. 085 x 0 m. 30 (pl. XXIV).

### 59491. Letter to Zenon from Patymis. — 0.33 m x 0.095 m (Plate XXV).

### 59492. Letter to Zenon from Paosis. — 0.175 m x 0.145 m.

Paosis, who had been put under Zenon’s protection by his father Horos, one of Apollonios’ sailors, complains that Herakleides, headman of the Philadelphian estate, has put him in prison for the purpose of exacting a hundred drachmae from him. ### 59493. Memorandum to Zenon from Pemenasis — 0.175 m $\times$ 0.185 m.

> The word *pasture* <note>original: νομὴν / nomēn</note> in line 12 shows that the writer was a herdsman of some sort. The door-keeper would not allow him to have access to Zenon, which was probably the reason why he presented a written petition. He complains of his hard situation and makes some excuses for himself for not being able to pay the dues which he owes. The text, however, is fragmentary and not quite intelligible as it stands.

<margin>2</margin> The door-keeper prevents us from coming to you, although

<margin>Line 1.</margin> *Pemenasis*: *P. S. I.* <note>Pubblicazioni della Società Italiana</note>, 368, 20 mentions a goatherd named Horus, son of Pemenasis, possibly miswritten for Pemenasis himself.
<margin>Line 2.</margin> I take *heōs* <note>until</note> in the sense of *teōs* <note>meanwhile/hitherto</note> (compare with no. 59367, 34 and Mayser, *Grammar*, II, p. 58), "though up till now we used to enter and speak to you." But we might put a comma before *four months* and translate, "and while we have been trying to petition you, four months have gone by."
