### 59495. Letter to Zenon from Petenouris and Samoys. — 0.13 m x 0.265 m (plate XXVI).

Two swineherds who had been put in prison for some fault do not deny that they have been rightly punished, but appeal to Zenon to have pity on them and liberate them, lest their herds should perish for want of their care and themselves perish through lack of the necessaries of life.
The petition is carefully written in a school hand <note>this refers to a slow, deliberate script often used by those not fully fluent in writing</note> with spaces between every two or three words and is composed of a string of short, dislocated clauses. It reads like the effort of one who had quite a good vocabulary, but not much skill in composition; or perhaps he was translating roughly from Egyptian into Greek.

To Zenon, greetings from Petenouris and Samoys, the swineherds. We beg 
you, then, have mercy on us; for we have been punished for the things in which 
we sinned; for no one is without sin; so that our sacrificial animals <note>original: *hiereia*; these were likely pigs intended for religious offerings or state revenue</note> may 
not perish while we are in want. You, therefore, make trial of us. You 
5 know that since we came, it is now the <gloss>eighth</gloss> third day; you do not release 
us
to work or to go to the animals, so that they might not perish while we 
are in prison. For we have nothing of the necessaries of life, 
but we are perishing here. You, therefore, look into this, if it seems good to you 
to release us. For we have no master but you. To you, therefore, 
10 we flee for refuge, so that we may obtain mercy.
->May you prosper.<-

Line 5. *aphieis*: 2nd person singular, present indicative <note>you release</note>.
Line 6. of us <note>original: *hēmōn*</note>: the papyrus has *hēmōi*, as there was not sufficient space to complete the letter *n*.

<term>BIBLIOGRAPHY</term>: Journal entry of the Museum, no. 49025.

### 59496. Letter from Petobastis to Zenon. — 0.11 m x 0.34 m (plate XXVII).

Petobastis, probably a farmer employed by Zenon, had been arrested by Hermaphilos the manager <note>original: *oeconome*; the chief financial official of the district</note> for some reason not clearly stated (see line 5). Hermaphilos refused to liberate him unless he received a request from Zenon, who appears to have taken little interest in the matter (if "you have been indifferent" <note>original: *katerrathy-mēkas*</note> is rightly read in line 2) and to have done nothing in answer to Petobastis’ previous appeals. Petobastis now sends a messenger to find him and get a letter from him to Hermaphilos, and he begs him to write at the same time to Python and Antipatros asking them to speak to the manager when the letter is delivered.
The papyrus cannot be earlier than the last years of the reign of King Philadelphos, about which time Hermaphilos seems to have succeeded Aristandros as the Arsinoite manager (see no. 59342).

Petobastis to Zenon, greetings. I have written to you many times about my situation so that 
you might write to Hermaphilos
to <gloss>me</gloss> release me from prison; but you have been indifferent, even though work 
is pressing upon us.
I supposed, therefore, that you would not [neglect me] so, [but] would take every care 
concerning me <gloss>you will take</gloss>; for Hermaphilos says he will not release me unless you write to him. For I have 
often sent him
5 petitions <note>original: *hypomnēmata*; formal requests or memoranda</note>. Know also that I have not been led away for a debt; for I have done 
what is right <note>meaning he has paid his dues</note> for the King. 
You would do well, then, to write him a letter so that I may be released; 
likewise also to Python 
and Antipatros write to them so that they may remind him at the same time as 
the letter from you is delivered
to him. I have also asked Nikaia to travel to you, so that you might give 
him a letter to Her-
maphilos; for they say he is about to go abroad to Memphis.
->Farewell.<-

Line 1. *grapsēis*: read as "you should write." So also in line 4.
Line 3. The letter before the gap looks like th, s, or ph; "to be at ease" <note>original: *ephēsychasein*</note> or "to drag out" <note>original: *ephelkysein*</note> would give the required sense, though neither is a certain restoration.
Line 5. "I have not been arrested on account of debt, for I have paid all I owe to the Crown."
Line 6. Python: the royal banker who lived in Krokodilopolis and knew the manager 
familiarly. Antipatros seems to have been his colleague (see no. 59503).
Line 7. *epistolē tēi*: corrected from "of the letter."
Line 8. *dōis*: for "you might give," as often in this period.
Line 9. "about to": the letter *m* written over *e*.

### 59497. Letter from Petobastis to Zenon. — 0.20 m x 0.21 m.

Probably by the author of no. 59496, though in a different hand. After an allusion to some affair which had brought on him a severe punishment — whether this is the same trouble as that of which he writes in no. 59496 is uncertain — Petobastis goes on to give an account of certain quantities of corn and sesame and ends by asking Zenon to think about the sowing of hay, as the flood-water is already receding from the land.

->Petobastis to Zenon, greetings.<-
->...to go to Crocodilopolis <note>original: *Krokodilōn polin*; the capital of the Fayum region</note><-
<margin>3</margin> ->I am [wary] of the collector <note>original: *praktoa*; likely refers to a tax or debt collector</note> [. .]ll[. . . . . . . . . .]i being 
forgiving; for I have been sufficiently and [bitterly] punished.<-
<margin>5</margin> ->I have also sent you the [account] according to which you also hold property in 
Philadelphia; and the assistant [from] Herakleides the grain-
collector has also written to you regarding the [grain measured] 
through me into the [granary] in the Village of the Syrians <note>original: *Syron komē*</note>. I have 
also sent Glaukias to you bringing 150 artabae <note>a Greek unit of dry capacity, roughly 30-40 liters</note> of sesame;
<margin>10</margin> ->and there are also in the granary 2 1/2 1/8 artabae. I have

for the hay-sowing.<-
->Farewell. [Year ...] Thoth 8.<-

<note>Line 3. original: *eulaboumai* (I am cautious) or *phoboumai* (I fear). The context suggests that "collector" is a mistake for "agent" (cf. also no. 59496), but without more evidence I do not venture to change it.</note>
<note>Line 7. assistant: original: *hypēretēs*. For Herakleides see no. 59314.</note>
<note>Line 8. Village of the Syrians: a village near Philadelphia (see P. Teb., II, p. 402).</note>
<note>Line 11. "together with the hay" would be too short and the letter before 'm' does not seem to be 'a'. Possibly "seed for hay" (original: *chortou sperma*); for the construction compare Anthologia Palatina, V, 40, 8, "and take care of a cloak for me."</note>

### 59499. A series of communications from Petosiris. — 0.14 m x 0.35 m and 0.135 m x 0.38 m (plate XXVIII).

The first document on the front <note>original: *recto*</note> is an account, written in large letters, of the sums received by Herieus the stone-cutter from the month of Athyr to Pharmouthi and of the sums earned by him, the balance to his debt being 313 1/3 drachmæ. Then follows a memorandum to Zenon (lines 27-43) about the above account and about other sums owed by Herieus, who seems to have been a somewhat unscrupulous person. The back <note>original: *verso*</note> contains a draft of a letter to Kleon (lines 44-83) and of another memorandum to Zenon (lines 84-101) on the subject of houses and of the conduct of a certain Pais; but the text is so mutilated and the Greek is so extraordinarily bad that it is difficult to give a clear account of what Petosiris means to say. The text has been pieced together out of half a dozen fragments acquired at different times.

<summary>This page contains letters to Zenon from subordinates: Petobastis reports on grain shipments and the urgency of sowing hay as the Nile flood recedes, while another Petobastis, a pigeon-keeper, pleads for four months of overdue wages and better quality grain rations.</summary>

<note>The following notes are printed in English at the bottom of the page.</note>

*Line 3.* In document no. 59296 we find Herieus in year 35 working on a shrine of the Samothracian gods, but there were many temples in Philadelphia and we cannot yet identify the present precinct. Was it that of the "Brother Gods" <note>original: *Theoi Adelphoi*, the deified Ptolemy II and Arsinoe II</note>? The wheat was probably for his workmen as well as himself (compare *Papyri Società Italiana*, 423, 17).
*Line 12.* "Wells" <note>original: *Phreta*</note> for "Wells" <note>original: *Phreata*</note> (compare *Papyri Società Italiana*, 423, 16).
*Lines 12-13.* "which... measured out": possibly ‘for those which Sostratos measured’ (compare *Papyri Società Italiana*, 423, 13), the meaning being that Herieus had not fulfilled his contract, for which he had been paid or partly paid in advance. But it is simpler to translate ‘for the corn which Sostratos measured out’.
*Lines 20-21.* The "royal stones" <note>original: *lithoi basilikoi*</note> are mentioned again in *Papyri Società Italiana*, 423. We learn from a fragment of another version of the same account that the "connecting stones," were from two to two and a half cubits long.

<note>The following notes are printed in English at the bottom of the page.</note>

*Lines 34-35.* The original text uses a misspelled form for "five months."
*Line 36.* "so that he may no longer try any more dodges": translated from the Greek expression meaning to shift or change one's position.
*Line 39.* "delivered them" <note>original: *aperithmesato*</note> seems here to mean ‘consigned them to Herieus’, who then entered them in the account as his own.
*Line 41.* "Sisinnes": likely intended to mean "from Sisinnes."
*Lines 42-43.* There is a horizontal line below line 42, while line 43 is added at the bottom of column 1. The original contains a spelling error in "separately from the calf."
*Lines 45-52.* ‘The house of Timoxenos, the bailiff came to sell it. Etearchos said, “I will buy it”. The sale is not yet ratified. If therefore you wish, buy it. Whatever money he bought it for, you will find in the house (its worth in) brick and wood’. But the last four lines might be punctuated and interpreted in different ways.

100 the castor-oil seeds <note>original: "kroton." The production of castor oil for lamps was a strictly regulated state monopoly</note>, and nowhere has he [[sold]] built a house except those which he has now sold.

*Lines 99-100*. Read: "to Horus, the one in charge of the castor-oil seeds" and compare with document no. 59243.

### 59500. Letter to Zenon from Pettukamis. — 0 m. 105 x 0 m. 21 (plate XXIV).

The writer, who was a potter from Sacred Island <note>original: "Hiera Nesos," a village in the Fayum</note> (compare *P. S. I.*, 420, 21), says that Zenon knows by experience whether or not he is an able workman. But if he is to be employed, he must have such assistants as will be useful to him. As an additional aid he proposes to engage Paesis and his sons, for he thinks highly of them and they are well acquainted with the ground. They must begin in the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly September/October</note>, in order that the work may be finished in good time and prove useful. He ends by asking to be shown the place in which he is to work. Presumably Pettukamis and the other potters were being engaged by Zenon to make jars for the use of the district under his control.

To Zenon, greetings from Pettukamis the potter from Sacred Island. You have
had experience of me, whether I am a skilled craftsman or not. Therefore, if I am to work,
it is necessary for me to retain with myself the craftsmen who are going to be
useful to me. I will also take on Paesis and his sons;
5 for I approve of them, and at the same time they are not inexperienced with the earth in that place <note>The writer likely refers to the specific clay quality of the area</note>.
And it is the right season to work from the month of Thoth, so that the works may be completed
without delay in due season and be useful at the same time. May you prosper.
And command that the place in which I am to work be shown to me.

*Line 1*. Sacred Island: a village near Philadelphia (*P. Teb.*, II, p. 380).
*Line 2*. "that" <note>original: "hina"</note>: the grammatical construction changes and the word is left without a following verb.
*Line 4*. Paesis: no doubt the author of document no. 59481.
*Line 5*. "earth" <note>original: "ges"</note>: Does this mean 'land' or 'clay'? <note>In the context of a potter, 'clay' is most probable</note>.
*Line 8*. This line has been added as a postscript.

*Bibliography*: *Journal of Entry of the Museum*, no. 49030.

### 59502. Letter from Ptolemaios to Zenon. — 0 m. 22 x 0 m. 12.

Ptolemaios informs Zenon of the settlement made by Phanias the scribe <note>original: "grammateus"</note> (see no. 59254) with the cavalrymen. He has liberated their crops, but made them undertake in future to present their horses in good condition at the inspection. Zenon may therefore send some one to take delivery of the sesame and the balance of barley owed by the cavalrymen, and he is requested to let Ptolemaios know whom he is sending.

It appears that the cavalrymen were obliged to maintain horses and that Phanias, finding some deficiency in their number or quality, would not let the crops be released from bond until he had received an assurance for the future. Part of the crops belonged to Zenon, whether he had advanced money on them or had helped to cultivate the land, and he had therefore a practical interest in Phanias’ decision and perhaps too some influence in the matter (compare no. 59254). *Line 4.* "He has released" <note>original: "apheoken"</note> (not "he sent away" <note>original: "apheeken," as printed by Rostovtzeff</note>): compare "they are forgiven" <note>original: "apheontai"</note> in the Gospel of *Luke* 5, 23.
*Lines 7-8.* "at the inspection... to present" <note>original: "epi tou arithmou... anastesai"</note>: compare *P. S. I.*, 495, 13-15, "for the inspection of the soldiers... and concerning the horse, he said he would see to it that it was presented for me." It was part of Phanias' duties to review <note>original: "arithmein"</note> the soldier-settlers <term>cleruchs; soldiers granted land in exchange for military service</term> in his district (compare no. 59254) and "to present" <note>original: "anastanai"</note> seems to be the technical word for showing a horse at the official inspection.
*Line 11.* "the [barley] among the cavalrymen": Rostovtzeff supposes this to refer to payments due to the State and collected by Zenon. But "he has released" in line 4 means the release of the crops apart from the amounts claimed by the State. Moreover, the parallel text *P. S. I.*, 360 says clearly "the grain still owed to you" and "so that they may settle their accounts with you."

## 59503. Letter from Python and Antipatros(?) to Panakestor. — 0 m. 115 X 0 m. 29 (plate XXIX).

It is unfortunate that this text is so mutilated, and the following interpretation is offered with the consciousness that it may be very wide of the mark. On the assumption that Python is the banker and that Antipatros is the person mentioned

<column-break/>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

along with him in no. 59496, I suggest that the subject of the letter is the distribution of banks controlled by the Treasury. Apollonios <note>The Dioiketes or Chief Minister of Finance under Ptolemy II</note>, the writers say, is now making a settlement with the managers <term>oiconomes; local financial officials</term> and has promised that he will afterwards settle with them, keeping the management of the king's bank in his own hands and giving them the banks depending on himself in the provinces <note>original: "nomos"</note>. The difficulty lies in the completion of the text after "the [bank] from the king." If I am right in understanding "bank" <note>original: "trapezan"</note>, the text yields some new information about the position of the banks in Ptolemaic Egypt. Compare *Revenue Laws*, columns 73-78. But admittedly the word to be supplied after "the [bank] from the king" may be something quite different, whether indicated in line 3 or in the previous correspondence. Apart from the double "greetings" in line 1, the letter bears signs of having been written by a hasty and careless scribe.

->with the managers<-

->And when he is finished with these, he has agreed with us to do business, and while he himself will take the bank<-
5 ->from the king and [[ <gloss>give,</gloss> ... ]] the ones from himself in the<-
->provinces<-

->To Panakestor.<-

*Line 1.* Antipatros: this was the name of Panakestor's father (*P. S. I.*, 509) and the writer may have been a relative.
*Line 3.* Possibly "making the management of the banks before the king." <note>original: "epi tou basileos ten oikonomian poioumenon ton trapezon"</note> But unluckily the line is almost illegible.
*Line 4.* "to do business" <note>original: "hemein poiesein"</note>: literally, 'will do for us.'
*Line 5.* Perhaps "to give [to no one]." <note>original: "metheni dosein"</note>

### 59507. Memorandum to Zenon from Pyrrhos. — 0 m. 33 X 0 m. 135.

Pyrrhos complains that from the time when Hermon sailed down the river he has received no allowance of money, corn or oil. When he was planning to sail down to Zenon and had no provision for the journey, his mother was obliged to pawn a <term>himation; an outer cloak or wrap</term> for 1 1/2 drachmae and Iason could scarcely be persuaded to give him 12 drachmae in Kerke. He asks Zenon therefore to order the arrears to be paid and the allowances to be given regularly in future and to see also that he receives the clothing allowance; and he promises that his conduct will be irreproachable. His mother also ought to be considered, as she too has received no salary for the last fourteen months. Finally he asks Zenon to order Iason to give them the hut of Apollodoros the late head of the smithy and also five rafters of seven cubits.
The mention of the allowances for the writer and his mother recalls the application of Kleon (no. 59457) and suggests that Pyrrhos was another of the youths whom Zenon was supporting and training in the <term>palaestra; a wrestling school or athletic training ground</term>, possibly the Pyrrhos who forms the subject of the letters nos. 59060 and 59061. These letters, however, were written in Alexandria, while the writer of the present memorandum was evidently living in the <term>chora; the rural districts of Egypt outside the capital</term>. Another possibility is that the author was Pyrrhos the farmer (see no. 59268).

->Memorandum to Zenon from<-
->Pyrrhos. Know that since<-
->Hermon sailed down...<-

### 59509. Letter to Zenon from Somoelis. — 0.19 m x 0.19 m.

Somoelis, the Jewish guard of the granary at Philadelphia, reports that he has sown a certain piece of land and that he is therefore entering in his account with Zenon twenty **artabs** <note>an ancient Egyptian unit of dry volume, roughly 30-40 liters</note> of wheat for the sowing. He complains of being oppressed by Etearchos and begs Zenon to write and ask him to be more considerate, and he offers to buy him 1000 artabs of barley from the cavalrymen. If possible, he would like to have an additional granary, the present one not being large enough to hold this year's crop. For guarding the granary there he receives nothing except an artab and a half of wheat per month given him by the inhabitants of Philadelphia, a pittance which does not even suffice to feed his children, unless he himself earns something extra.

<summary>This page contains petitions and letters to Zenon regarding unpaid wages, food allowances, and logistical requests, including a notable mention of a Jewish granary guard named Somoelis. These documents reveal the personal financial hardships and the system of patronage among the employees of the Apollonios estate.</summary>

<margin>2</margin> [the land the]re [at] Amande... There are, then, belonging to you from me 20 **artabae** <term>artaba: a Persian unit of dry capacity used in Egypt, roughly 30 to 40 liters</term> of **wheat** <gloss>belonging</gloss>

<margin>7</margin> [that we may not] be wronged. [I] am also able to purchase for you 1,000 artabae of **barley** <note>original: "krithes"</note>

*Line 1.* Somoelis: to be distinguished from Somoelis the vine-dresser (no. 59367).
*Line 2.* Amande...: perhaps a proper name followed by "land."
*Lines 4-5.* The verb might be "broke" <note>original: "ἐπέκλα[σεν"</note> or "summoned" <note>original: "ἐπεκάλ[εσεν"</note> and the letter after the gap in line 5 might be *i* or *n*. "[the so]n" or "[the stra]nger" would suit the space.
*Line 8.* cavalrymen: read cavalrymen <note>original: "ἱππέων"</note>. Apparently he did not wish to buy from the peasants in case there might be some unsettled claims against them.

### 59517. Account from Timanthes. — 0.255 m. x 0.12 m.

Timanthes, who appears again as an overseer of farm hands in *P. Hamb.*, I, 114, gives an account of the money spent in wages to workmen who have been engaged to collect the dry sticks from the fields, burn out the old stumps and cut down the brushwood. These operations lasted from the 25th of Thoth to the 9th of Phaophi, after which the workmen were turned on to irrigate the land thus cleared. The daily wage was 3/4 of an obol per head, no doubt a common rate for this sort of labor.

> From Timanthes:
> account from the 20 drachmae of the 
> clearing of land. Thoth 26: for 
> collection of brushwood and burning:
> 8 persons at 3/4 obol each = 1 drachma.
> <margin>5</margin> 26th: 4 persons. 27th: 4 persons.
> 28th: 7 persons. 29th: 8 persons = 1 drachma.
> 30th: 4 persons. Phaophi 1st:
> for the spreading brushwood:
> 12 persons = 1 1/2 drachmae.
> <margin>10</margin> 6th: for collection and burning:
> 9 [persons] = 1 drachma 1 1/2 obols. 6th: 7 persons.
> 6th: 6 persons.
> 7th: 7 persons. 8th: 5 persons.
> 9th: 5 persons. Total: 16 drachmae and some obols.

Line 8. The verb might be read as "entrusting" <note>original: "ἐπιτρέπουσαν"</note>, but "spreading over" <note>original: "ἐπιτρέχουσαν"</note> gives a more satisfactory sense, 'the brushwood spreading over the fields'.

### 59520. Petition to Zenon from Pharates. — 0.145 m. $\times$ 0.34 m. (pl. XXX).

Pharates the beekeeper had a dispute with another beekeeper named Maieus. Maieus had previously appealed to Zenon, who provided him with a letter to Noumenios in Akanthopolis. Following Zenon's instructions, Noumenios and the local elders heard the case and issued a judgment. However, Maieus refused to accept the ruling and insisted the case be brought back before Zenon for a final decision. While the next part of the papyrus is difficult to read, it appears Maieus conspired with a man named Limnaios, who threw Pharates into prison to prevent him from making his own appeal to Zenon. Despite this, Pharates is ready to provide legal guarantors and face Maieus in court. He begs Zenon not to leave him in prison; he has been held for twenty-two days already, and the season has arrived for moving the beehives to their seasonal pastures.

there, then, before Numenios
and before the elders. But he did not abide by <unclear>that</unclear> judgment, but said he would be judged before
5 Zenon. But I <unclear>was</unclear> <note>the text here is highly fragmented and the sense is lost</note>...

*Line 1. Maieus: compare with no. 59466.*
*Line 3. Numenios may be the <term>phylakites: a guard or policeman</term> mentioned in no. 59475, or else an <term>epistates: a local administrative official</term> presiding with a council of elders. This village justice had no legal force and one of the parties declined to be bound by it.*
*Line 4. Possibly "not in any way," <note>original: "οὐ[δὲ κα]τ’ οὐδέν"</note> though the ending might be a verb. "He did not pay attention" <note>original: "προσέσχεν"</note> does not seem a possible reading.*
*Line 6. Read "communicates to Limnaios." The preceding words seem to be a reported speech of Maieus.*
*Line 7. The hives belonged to a temple of Isis and seem to have formed a subject of recrimination between the two beekeepers. The mention of Isis recalls "Meieus the keeper of the Temple of Isis" <note>original: "Μειεῦς Ἰσιονόμος"</note> of no. 59172, 14, but there is nothing else to identify him with the Maieus of the present text.*
*Line 8. "Having provided sureties": probably for "remaining in place" <note>original: "παραμονῆς"</note>, the sureties being responsible for the appearance of Pharates at the trial if he were now released from prison.*
*Line 10. The last letters might be "as I am able" <note>original: "οὗ ἂν δύνωμαι"</note> or "us."*

### 59522. Letter from Philinos to Zenon. — 0.345 m. x 0.11 m.

Philinos asks Zenon to receive from Herakleides 250 <term>artabs: a measure of dry volume, roughly 30–40 liters</term> of wheat and 300 of barley, and also the corn which he bought in partnership with Philinos for 100 drachmae, whatever the amount was; and he is to keep these quantities together in order that they may give the barley to Artemidoros and keep the wheat. Zenon is requested to choose corn of as good quality as possible and send specimens to Philinos. He is also to give Dionysios an allowance of bread and wine for every day that he stays with him and to look after his comfort.

For Philinos see no. 59363. The present text shows that there was a close business connection between the two men.

Philinos to Zenon
greetings. Have
measured out from
Herakleides 250 artabs of wheat
5 and 300 artabs of barley
and those which you bought
with us for 100 drachmae,
however many you bought,
and keep these in the
10 same place...

*Lines 4-8. "Those which... you bought" depends on "Have measured out," not on "keep." The corn had been bought previously, so many artabs for 100 drachmae, but had not been measured out from the granary.*
*Line 9. "These" <note>original: "ταυ"</note> corrected from "those" <note>original: "τας"</note>.*

> and pressed grapes to be 
> packed, so they might have sour wine; and 
> 10 now I have written to you again. You will do 
> well to give them to him. For the men are

<note>Line 4. We wrote: or perhaps "I wrote indeed" (cf. no. 59305, 1).</note>
<note>Lines 8-9. To be packed: the reading of the Greek word is uncertain.</note>

## 59528. Petition to Zenon from Chesthotes(?). — 0 m. 145 X 0 m. 145.

The writer had apparently lent 284 <term>drachmae: the standard currency of the Greek world (original symbol: "⊢")</term>, the loan being confirmed by the royal oath, to another Egyptian on condition that if he did not return the money by a certain time he would be liable to exaction. The money not having been repaid, Zenon is asked to write to the proper authorities. The petition seems to have been of the same form as those addressed to the king.

> To Zenon, greetings, from Chesthotes. 
> [I am being wronged] by Oaphres son of Inaros 
> [concerning a loan] confirmed by the oath of King Ptolemy 
> [for] 284 drachmae, on the condition that if he does not pay back [ . . .
> 5 and now, the time having 
> passed, [I beg you,] if it seems good to you, to write [ . . .

<note>Line 1. At the end of the line read "I am being wronged" (adikoumai).</note>
<note>Line 5. At the end of the line read "I beg you therefore" (deomai oun).</note>

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Journal of Entries of the Museum*, no. 49056.

---

## 59529. Fragment of letter from Horos to Zenon. — 0 m. 085 X 0 m. 10.

Horos "the one in charge of the castor-oil plant" of nos. 59243 and 59499 is probably to be distinguished from the assistant and sub-architect of nos. 59291, 59531 and *P. S. I.*, 625.

> Horos to Zenon, greetings.
> An unpleasantness has occurred to me
> with Demetrios. For when 
> Artemidoros had 
> 5 written concerning the building
> where the breeder was, he said no...

<note>Line 6. The breeder: perhaps the stallion kept by Artemidoros the physician (no. 59225).</note>

BIBLIOGRAPHY: *Journal of Entries of the Museum*, no. 49057.

**59531. Memorandum to Zenon from Horos.** — 0 m. 25 x 0 m. 10.

Hedylos the <term>architekton</term> <note>A chief engineer or overseer of public works</note> (see no. 59247) had forbidden Horos to attend to the works, but the latter insists that it is his business to keep an account of the bricks furnished by the brickmakers (cf. no. 59291). Nearly half the text is missing and I have restored it provisionally in accordance with the above interpretation.

> Memorandum to Zenon from Horos.
> Hedylos has forbidden me, saying, "Do not 
> approach the [works ... so that] 
> we [might not] find you at the [building site]."
> <margin>5</margin> But now, know [that I am following] 
> the [bricks] hauled
> to the drying ground <note>original: ψυγμοῦ</note> [and those] 
> brought by the [brick-carriers]. 
> If therefore I do not [follow the bricks]
> <margin>10</margin> being hauled and [those being] 
> brought, and [receive] the
> receipt [every day] from Petos [who has undertaken] 
> the works, 
> I cannot [oversee the]
> <margin>14</margin> works. [I have written] these things [to you]
> <margin>16</margin> so that you may know [that I am approaching] 
> the works [and] you may manage [concerning] 
> these matters.
> Farewell. Year 31 <note>The 31st year of Ptolemy II Philadelphus's reign, approx. 255 BCE</note>.

Line 2. Read **Hedylos** and **approach**.
Lines 3-4. Perhaps **that we might not find you**.
Line 7. **drying ground**: "the ψυγμοῦ". For the double gamma see Mayser, *Grammar*, I, p. 217.
Line 19. Probably **31** or **34**.

**BIBLIOGRAPHY:** Journal of Entries of the Museum, no. 49059.

## VIII. — SYMBOLS.

->Monograms and abbreviations whose meaning is not self-evident are resolved in the text or explained in the notes. The following conventional signs are assumed to be known :<-

| | | | |
|:---:|---|:---:|---|
| L | year. | — | obol. |
| L | of this, of these or from this, from these. | = | two-obols. |
| / | total, totals. | ϛ | three-obols. |
| ∠ | 1/2. | ϛ — | four-obols. |
| β', γ', δ' etc. | 2/3, 1/3, 1/4, etc. | ϛ = | five-obols. |
| 𐅿 <br> β | 900. | c | half-obol. |
| Μ̂, Μ, etc. | 10,000, 20,000, etc. | 𐅵 | quarter (1/4 of an obol). |
| λ̅ | talent. | χ, χ, etc. | of copper and 1, 2, etc. copper coins, choinikes, choes according to the context. <note>Units of volume for dry or liquid goods</note> |
| ⊢ | drachma. | | |

<summary>This index listing provides English translations for Greek terms used in the Zenon Papyri, primarily those starting with the prefix "epi-" and "en-". These terms are essential for understanding the bureaucratic, legal, and economic systems of Ptolemaic Egypt, including tax assessments, land management, and formal petitions.</summary>
<keywords>Zenon Papyri, Greek vocabulary, Ptolemaic Egypt, land tax, legal terminology, agricultural rent, olive oil trade, formal petitions</keywords>

--- Page 142 ---
<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index of Greek terms found in the Zenon Papyri collection within the Cairo Museum Catalogue. The entries continue the letter epsilon (ε) and move into zeta (ζ) and eta (η). These terms reflect the extensive administrative, agricultural, and social vocabulary of the 3rd-century BCE estate, including references to letter-writing, labor, timekeeping, and common closing formulas used in correspondence.</meta>

With regard to lines 3-7, I suggest, in accordance with my former explanation, that they should be restored somewhat as follows: <note>The following Greek text explains the capacity of storage jars</note> "And the jar is as it were a sixteen-*chous* <note>a *chous* is about 3 liters</note> measure, so that there are ... in the twelve-*kotyle* measure ..., and the total measures are 888..." <note>original: τὸ δὲ κεράμιον ὡς ἐκκαιδεκά- / χουν ἐστίν, ὥστε γίνεσθαι τομ.......... τῶι δωδεκακοτύλωι........, τοὺς / δὲ πάντας μετρητὰς ωπη κτλ.</note> In line 13 what I wrongly read as a number γα is the end of a verb such as "we have received" <note>original: "κεκομίσμεθα"</note>, and the two lines which I placed at the foot of column 1 really belong to the top of column 2.

**59182**. A small, but important fragment of lines 20-25, which makes the text more intelligible and nullifies part of my explanation. It is probable that more fragments of the same papyrus will come to light.

**59257**, right side. The text is now almost complete.

> Year 39, the 9th of Phaophi. Asclepiades <note>original: "Ἀσκληπιάδης"</note>,
> a Lycian and one of Nikanor’s settlers <note>term: <term>klerouchos</term> — a soldier-colonist who received a plot of land from the state</note>, acknowledges that he has
> a loan from Zenon, the son of Agreophon, a Kaunian
> of the staff of Apollonios the finance minister <note>term: <term>dioiketes</term> — the highest financial official in Ptolemaic Egypt</note>,

> of Asclepiades, who authorized it.

**59294**. Another large fragment has been recovered, showing the document to be a memorandum addressed to Zenon by Horos, probably the stone-cutter <note>original: "λατόμος"</note> mentioned in *P. S. I.*, 423, about the balancing of accounts. The text is still very incomplete and I postpone the publication of it for the present, trusting that the missing portions will turn up before long.

**59312**, 12. As the following dates in lines 16-18 are presumably of Epeiph, perhaps after all it is better to read "in the month of Pachon" <note>original: "τῶι Παχῶνoς"</note>.

**59319**, 10. A slave called Pindaros belonging to Apollonios is mentioned in a British Museum papyrus (see Rostovtzeff, *Large Estate*, p. 20).

**59320**, 3. Compare *P. Alex.* 292, published by M. Norsa in *Bulletin* no. 23, p. 273: "the distinctive mark of Isis" <note>original: "παρδση(μος) Ἴσις"</note>.

**59326**, 62. "he reports having given" <note>original: "ἀναφέρει δεδωκώς"</note>: for the meaning and construction compare "he reports having received" <note>original: "φέρει παρειληφώς"</note> (59147, 4) and "he reports having smelted" <note>original: "φέρει κεχωνευκώς"</note> (unpublished). "To carry" <note>original: "φέρειν"</note> and "to carry up/back" <note>original: "ἀναφέρειν"</note> are used indiscriminately in the sense of to report.

<column-break/>

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>ZENON PAPYRI.</header>

**59326**, 175. In view of *P. Petr.* II, 28, column 8, 13 perhaps we ought to read "to Oaphres" <note>original: "Ὀαφρῆι," a Greek rendering of the Egyptian name Apries</note> rather than "to Oaphies," although the fourth letter looks more like an 'i' <note>iota</note> than an 'r' <note>rho</note>.

**59333**, 79. The word to be supplied is probably "list" or "inventory" <note>original: "γραφή"</note>.

**59346**, 8, note. Instead of ‘inscribed’ read ‘marked’.

**59412**, 19, note. Read ‘I am pressing him’.

**59466**, 5. Perhaps "we shall be put away" <note>original: "ἀποθησόμεθα"</note> is to be understood as a passive, ‘we shall be put in prison’.

**59477**, 16. "to procure" <note>original: "πορίσαι"</note>: the note is to be cancelled, as there is good authority for the use of the active voice in the sense of ‘procure for oneself’.

**59503**, 6. Instead of "the things being heard" <note>original: "τὰ ἀκο(υ)όμεν(α)"</note>, I think it is better to read "the four things we hear" <note>original: "τὰ ἀκο(ύ)ομεν," taking "τὰ" as a mistake for "d̅," the numeral for 4</note>.

See also a series of important remarks and corrections by Wilcken in the last number of the *Archive for Papyrus Research* <note>original: "Archiv für Papyrusforschung"</note>. I regret that I did not see these until it was too late to study and utilize them in the present volume.

## PLATE XXIV

*This page consists of a high-quality photographic reproduction showing two distinct papyrus fragments recovered from the Zenon Archive. These documents, preserved for over two millennia in the dry sands of Egypt, represent the daily administrative "paperwork" of a large Ptolemaic estate.*

<image-desc>
The plate displays two dark-colored papyrus fragments. The organic fibers of the reeds are clearly visible, creating a grid-like texture behind the ink. The handwriting is in Ancient Greek cursive, a style of script used for rapid business and personal correspondence rather than formal literature.
</image-desc>

<margin>59488</margin>
<image-desc>
**Fragment 59488 (left):** This is a long, narrow vertical strip of papyrus, often called a "narrow format" scroll, typical of shorter memos or lists. It contains roughly 20–25 lines of Greek text written in a compact, fluent cursive hand <note>Fluent cursive indicates a professional scribe who could write quickly and efficiently</note>. The text runs horizontally across the width of the strip. The fragment shows some mechanical damage, with small holes and frayed edges at the top and bottom, likely where the scroll was most exposed to the elements.
</image-desc>

<column-break/>

<margin>59500</margin>
<image-desc>
**Fragment 59500 (right):** A larger, roughly rectangular fragment. It contains approximately 10 lines of continuous Greek cursive text. The handwriting here is slightly larger and more spaced out than the first fragment, suggesting a different scribe or perhaps a more formal piece of correspondence. There is a clear margin on the right side of the piece, indicating where the scribe ended their lines. The edges are irregular and worn, showing the natural decay of the material over time.
</image-desc>

<summary>This page contains an administrative memorandum from the Zenon Archive detailing the settlement of silver debts (measured in drachmae and obols) and the management of estate resources like oil and indigo. It specifically references the "produce of the 26th year," placing the document in the mid-3rd century BCE during the management of the estate of Apollonios.</summary>
<keywords>Zenon Archive, accounting, drachma, obol, indigo dye, olive oil, Ptolemaic Egypt, tax settlement, produce, Menon</keywords>

# CATALOGUE OF THE CAIRO MUSEUM — ZENON PAPYRI, VOL. III.
## PLATE XXIX

<margin>59303</margin>

<image-desc>
A black and white photograph of a large, vertically oriented papyrus fragment. The papyrus is dark and heavily damaged with several large white voids—known as <term>lacunae|missing sections of a manuscript caused by physical decay</term>—where the material has been lost. It contains multiple columns of Greek cursive text written in dark ink. The horizontal and vertical fiber patterns of the papyrus, which were used by ancient scribes to guide their pens, are clearly visible.
</image-desc>

*This plate displays Cairo inventory number 59303. The document is a significant example of a multi-columnar register or account from the Zenon Archive. The handwriting is a practiced, fluid cursive, suggesting it was produced by a professional scribe within the administration of Apollonios, the finance minister of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.*

<note>The Zenon Archive is one of the most important collections of papyri from the Hellenistic period, providing an intimate look at the economy and daily life in the Fayum region of Egypt.</note>

<meta>The inventory number "59303" is printed vertically in the right margin. There is a small circular stamp or logo at the bottom right corner, followed by the printer's mark.</meta>

<image-desc>Small circular emblem containing stylized initials or a symbol.</image-desc>

Printed by the Catala Brothers, Paris. <note>original: "IMP. CATALA FRÈRES, PARIS."</note>

<summary>This plate provides a high-resolution facsimile of Cairo papyrus 59303, a large administrative document featuring multiple columns of Greek cursive script. It serves as a visual record of the bureaucratic accounting methods used in the 3rd century BCE Egyptian countryside.</summary>

<keywords>Zenon Papyri, Cairo Museum 59303, Greek cursive, administrative records, Ptolemaic bureaucracy, lacunae, Catala Brothers</keywords>
